articles.title: The Narrow Path to a Xi-Trump AI Deal
articles.body:
When Donald Trump arrived in Beijing in May, Xi Jinping was already on the offensive. The Chinese leader wasted zero time in rebuking his U.S. counterpart over arms sales to Taiwan directly warning that simmering tensions over the self-ruling island could ultimately cause the superpowers to “enter into conflict.”
Trump acquiesced. He delayed a $14 billion arms package to Taiwan, said future weapons would be discussed as a “very good negotiating chip” with Beijing, questioned the island’s sovereignty as something “nobody knows how to define,” and stressed that he was not looking to fight a war “9,500 miles away”—all without securing any apparent reduction in Chinese military pressure in return.
While this response alarmed many in democratic Taiwan, many people around the globe hope that Xi can prove similarly persuasive on another issue of grave importance when he travels to the White House on Sept 24: artificial intelligence.
“Taiwan is not a priority anymore,” Wang Yiwei, director of the Institute of International Affairs at Beijing's Renmin University, says of Xi’s impending visit. “The priority is definitely AI.”
In recent days, warnings from a whistleblower researcher and reports of rogue agent swarms have intensified fears of a doomsday scenario born of unbridled AI development. On Sept. 12, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay titled We Must Pace the Frontier calling for embedded independent evaluators, common safety standards among democracies, and eventually verifiable global coordination to slow dangerous frontier-AI development. OpenAI’s Sam Altman and SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk also voiced broad support for slowing frontier development.
However, one major skeptic is Trump, who responded on Truth Social that “AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX.” Moreover, he insisted that “President Xi, of China, just announced that China will be doing absolutely nothing to stand in the way of AI, or its future.”
That characterization is misleading. China regulates AI more stringently than most other countries, and already enforces AI security guidance, ethics review requirements, and binding obligations on consumer AI services. Xi has also publicly called for legal, technical, and ethical guardrails that keep AI under human control (albeit while resisting restrictions that could impede China’s technological rise). “We should strengthen risk-awareness and ensure that AI is secure and controllable,” he told the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai on July 17.
The hope among safety advocates is that Xi and Trump might strike a deal on AI. While Trump’s first term was anchored in antipathy to China, he posed a notably different tone in Beijing, calling Xi “a man I respect greatly” and telling him that “it’s an honor to be your friend.” Although that cordiality does not erase the national competition that makes either side hesitant to constrain its technological development, it may put narrower cooperation on the table.
Certainly, the moment is ripe to build a framework built on competition, cooperation, and strict guardrails. Beyond economic rivalry, both Washington and Beijing share an urgent interest in mitigating catastrophic miscalculations, particularly surrounding AI integration into defense architectures and nuclear command and control systems.
Trump also enters the summit under pressure, with soaring energy prices from the Iran war adding to voter discontent ahead of the midterms. “Trump needs a win more than Xi does,” says Jonathan Sullivan, head of China programs at the Asia Research Institute at the University of Nottingham.
Still, Xi’s motivations require clear-eyed scrutiny. Last week, Chen Yixin, China’s Minister of State Security, published an article in China Cyberspace Magazine that expounded upon the opportunities and challenges of AI. The top “risk,” he said, was “political security, institutional security, and ideological security.”
While the deeply paranoid Chinese Communist Party (CCP) won’t allow its people to access Google or Facebook, it cannot countenance AI exhibiting the kind of autonomy that was on display in July. That month, a “swarm” of OpenAI agents circumvented sandbox controls, communicated through unauthorized channels, gained access to AI platform Hugging Face, compromised credentials, and accessed internal datasets while trying to game evaluations. It’s enough to give a regime built on control pause.
But while China’s motivations may be driven as much by safeguarding party control as by addressing broader risks to humanity, these objectives can overlap. “If they go beyond bilateral competition and address so many concerns about AI development, that would show the co-leadership of China and the U.S.,” says Wang. “Not just two superpowers, but also two civilizations.”
However, any agreement requires overcoming profound distrust. Even as Amodei argued for pacing frontier AI development, he framed it in terms of competing with China, whose “lead in AI would pose grave danger for the United States and the world.” On that score, he advocated stronger export controls on advanced semiconductors, a crackdown on chip smuggling, and greater efforts to prevent Chinese companies from “distilling” the capabilities of Western models.
The contradiction of calling for a slowdown while talking up the “race” narrative wasn’t lost on critics (who also pointed out that Anthropic could temper its own research without external intervention). Others suggested that because cheap, open-weight Chinese AI models are among the chief rivals to Anthropic’s proprietary models, its CEO’s call to crack down on Chinese AI development could be seen as commercially motivated rather than altruistic—especially as the firm eyes a potential record-breaking IPO that could value the company at $2 trillion.
Indeed, China was quick to leap on Amodei’s essay as an example of “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition [that] will only hamper efforts toward sound global AI governance, which serves no one’s interest,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said last week. A flurry of strident op-eds in state media followed, with the CCP mouthpiece Global Times calling the essay a “‘Cold War script’ for the AI field.”
Amodei has long been a bête noire in Beijing for painting AI as a tussle between democracies and autocracies that casts China as the principal threat. “If there's ever a proposal that requires Chinese buy-in, the last person on earth that would be a good salesman is Dario Amodei,” says Ryan Hass, an expert in U.S.-China relations at the Brookings Institution.
But Amodei’s framing of AI as a zero-sum contest is far from an outlier—it is shared by a large chunk of the Trump administration. “There is no day after tomorrow if China wins at this,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sept. 8. “If they were to pull away from us on AI, then nothing else would matter.”
A grand bargain to slow AI development is unlikely, and grievances over distillation or export controls could stall negotiations. But experts see room for narrower cooperation. Both countries face threats from non-state actors using AI to sabotage infrastructure, mount cyberattacks, or create biological weapons, argues Alvin W. Graylin, a digital fellow at Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab. Sharing information about those threats could benefit both sides.
When Bessent met Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng and chief trade negotiator Li Chenggang on Sunday to thrash out summit objectives, he reportedly proposed a formal AI dialogue and a mechanism for each side to notify the other of AI incidents which threaten national security. Modest a measure it may be, it would be an important step towards avoiding some of the worst risks, says Scott Singer, a fellow and co-director of the China AI Initiative at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. “I wouldn’t take these small but critical steps for granted.”
Such a channel could help either side respond during a crisis, and reduce the risk of mistaking a non-state actor or rogue AI as an act of aggression. Reminiscent of the “red phone” that connected Washington to Moscow during the Cold War, experts have floated the idea of a literal fax machine to avoid mistranslations.
To be sure, Beijing has not publicly endorsed the proposal. Even if it does, important questions remain. What, for example, would classify a national security threat? Its effectiveness would also depend on whether governments learned of serious incidents. OpenAI only reported its agents' autonomous cyberattack after Hugging Face, the target of the attack, reported the breach to the FBI. Independent researchers have since uncovered other apparent instances of OpenAI agents compromising websites.
Beyond the proposed channel, Bessent has said the two countries have agreed to establish a recurring dialogue. Who will staff those talks, and how often they will meet, remains unclear. More than two years elapsed between the last official AI dialogue and Sunday’s meeting.
With the stakes quickly rising, Singer says another prolonged hiatus from the negotiating table could prove disastrous. “Who knows where we’re going to be in June 2027,” he says with respect to AI development. “This cannot go off the rails.”

articles.title: Saudis may seek help from Israel as current alliances prove insufficient against Houthis - analysis
articles.body:
The sharp escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has raised concerns that the confrontation could spread further across the region, with Washington worried that the conflict could intensify and potentially lead the Houthis to resume direct attacks on Israel, diplomatic officials told Maariv on Tuesday.
The officials said the key question is whether the situation can be brought under control or whether the confrontation will continue to escalate. Among the regional consequences being considered is the possibility that the Houthis could again try to attack Israel directly, as they did last year.
The concerns come after the US State Department updated its security guidance for American citizens in the Middle East, warning that the military confrontation between the Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia could escalate rapidly. The US Embassy in Israel also issued an alert urging citizens to remain vigilant and consider the possibility of flight disruptions, airspace closures, and transportation disruptions.
Diplomatic officials stressed that the updated and expanded warnings should not necessarily be seen as a sign that immediate developments are expected. The wording, they said, also reflects the administration's responsibility to warn American citizens in the region and make clear the seriousness of the situation should the confrontation intensify.
The warnings come against the backdrop of the latest escalation in the confrontation. Saudi Arabia confirmed that the Houthis launched a ballistic missile toward Riyadh, which was intercepted by the Saudi air defense system.
It was the first time the Saudi capital had been targeted since the current wave of escalation began. Residents reported hearing an explosion, and smoke was later seen near Riyadh's airport. No casualties or damage were reported.
The Houthis claimed they attacked "sensitive targets" in Riyadh with missiles and drones, as well as facilities belonging to oil giant Aramco in Yanbu. Saudi Arabia said it had also thwarted attempts to strike civilian infrastructure in Yanbu, Taif, Baish, and the Farasan Islands. Houthi claims that Aramco facilities were hit have not been verified.
Saudis divide efforts between defending territory, Red Sea shipping
The wave of attacks has forced Saudi Arabia to divide its efforts between defending cities and infrastructure from missiles and drones, securing energy facilities, and protecting shipping routes in the Red Sea.
In recent months, the Houthis have expanded their attacks on Saudi Arabia and shipping in the region, and in July they declared a naval blockade against the kingdom. Any disruption to traffic through the Bab al-Mandab Strait could significantly increase the economic and strategic cost of the confrontation.
Amid the tensions, US President Donald Trump returned to the White House from Camp David earlier than planned. No official explanation was given for the schedule change, and no confirmation links his early return to developments in the Middle East.
The return came as discussions were underway in Washington over the desired extent of US involvement in the confrontation. US media reported that options for action against the Houthis were examined while Trump was at Camp David, but no US decision to launch a strike was announced.
Washington has so far refrained from direct military intervention alongside Saudi Arabia in the current round of fighting and has not agreed to Riyadh's request to take military action against the Houthis.
Israel is closely monitoring developments. Israeli officials believe the pressure facing Saudi Arabia could also affect Riyadh's diplomatic calculations.
"Such an escalation could actually help the Abraham Accords," the officials said.
Israeli officials: Saudis recognizing alliances insufficient for Houthi threat
According to the officials, the Saudis are under pressure and are discovering that the relationships and alliances they have built are not currently providing a complete response to the threat. If the Houthi threat intensifies and the assistance the kingdom receives from its allies remains limited, they assess that Israeli capabilities could carry greater weight in the eyes of the Saudi leadership.
Saudi Arabia has been working in recent weeks to secure outside assistance. According to reports, amid a shortage of interceptors, it has requested air-defense assistance from France, the UK, Pakistan, and Egypt.
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman also traveled to Cairo and, according to the reports, sought Egyptian support against the Houthis.
Security cooperation among Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan is also being tested by developments on the ground.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Ankara was prepared to assist with Saudi military needs under the defense agreement among the three countries. Pakistan has so far not joined military action against the Houthis.
The gap between Riyadh's security needs and the assistance it is actually receiving is at the heart of the Israeli assessment. Israeli officials point in this context to the experience and capabilities Israel has accumulated in intelligence and air defense against the Houthis.
As the campaign continues, they assess that those capabilities could also become part of Saudi Arabia's broader considerations.

articles.title: Middle East live: Yemen fighting escalates as Trump heads to UN
articles.body:
Middle East live: Trump warns Iran to reach deal with US or face 'annihilation'
US President Donald Trump warned that he could "annihilate the Islamic Republic" if it failed to reach a peace deal with Washington in his UN General Assembly speech on Tuesday, calling on all nations to economically isolate Iran. The king of Saudi Arabia earlier denounced Yemen's Houthis as a "terrorist militia" in a rare statement, reacting to an attack authorities said targeted the holy city of Mecca last week. Follow our liveblog for the latest developments.
Live: Follow the debate
To display this content from , you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
US official met with the Iranian delegation for three hours
Turkey's Erdogan urges world to 'immediately' start rebuilding Gaza
The world must "immediately" start the reconstruction of the devastated Gaza Strip, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said.
"We must begin the reconstruction of Gaza immediately," he told the United Nations General Assembly, urging world leaders to "exert greater pressure on Israel".
Israel's relentless bombardment and ground offensive have devastated the Palestinian territory, damaging or destroying 84 percent of all structures as of October 2025.
Despite a US-brokered ceasefire, Israel has continued its air strikes and restricted entry of equipment that international NGOs say are needed for the territory's reconstruction, which has yet to begin.
According to a joint assessment published by the United Nations, the World Bank and the European Union in April, Gaza will require $71.4 billion in recovery and reconstruction spending over the next decade.
Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt affirm Riyadh's right to defend itself
The foreign ministers of Turkey, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan said in a joint statement that they affirmed Riyadh's right to defend itself in line with international law and stressed the need to maintain safety of navigation in the region. Yemen's Houthis have stepped up their attacks against Saudi Arabia as they secure their hold on the Bab al-Mandab strait.
Following a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, the ministers also expressed deep concern over the ongoing conflicts in the region, saying dialogue and diplomacy were the only pat to a sustainable solution. They also voiced their support for Yemen's internationally recognised government in its efforts to achieve stability and peace.
Turkey's Erdogan urges wider recognition of Palestinian state
Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan has condemned the situation in Gaza in his address to the UN General Assembly, saying "nobody with a conscience can close their eyes" to what is happening there.
He said he was saddened by Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas' absence from the gathering and urged countries that do not recognise a Palestinian state to review their position.
Jordan's King Abdullah condemns forced displacement of Palestinians in West Bank
Speaking after Trump, Jordan’s King Abdullah focuses on the "extraordinarily dangerous" events unfolding in the West Bank.
"Some may think we have seen this before settlements, violence, displacement, more of the same. But it is not. Nor is it simply an escalation. This is a fundamental shift," he says.
He adds that attacks on Palestinians in the occupied West Bank are not isolated acts but rather "elements of a single policy to compel an entire population to leave their land. And there is a name for that: forced displacement. And that is a war crime."
Trump warns he could 'annihilate' Iran without peace deal
With his speech at the UN, Trump has again attempted to justify his war with Iran, claiming it ensured Tehran would never obtain a nuclear weapon.
The US president warned that he could "annihilate the Islamic Republic" if no deal is reached to end the conflict, while predicting his administration would strike a peace deal with Iran following the November midterm elections.
Trump also called on other nations to join America in isolating Iran economically to force it to the negotiating table.
"I have a big decision to make. Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?" Trump said. "Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?"
He has previously cited a range of reasons for the February US-Israeli strikes, including Tehran's nuclear programme, its support for regional proxy groups and the prospect of regime change.
Trump calls for all ICC member countries to quit the international tribunal
The US president criticises an array of UN-backed organisations as "leftist" and "globalist", including the International Criminal Court.
"I call on all nations that are members of the ICC to officially resign from this rogue institution immediately," he tells the UNGA.
Trump's administration has prepared sanctions against the entire court and plans to announce them soon, sources familiar with the matter said ahead of the UN gathering.
The Trump administration has made no secret of its disdain for the global tribunal that prosecutes war crimes and genocide worldwide – and has worked to undermine it.
US officials want the court to drop its arrest warrants against Israeli leaders as well as a past probe into American troops in Afghanistan.
Replay: 'Military power alone cannot secure peace', says outgoing UN Secretary General
Speaking before Trump, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres pleaded for “a world built on interdependence” as he made his final UNGA address.
Guterres also rebuked might-makes-right thinking, telling superpowers to recognize “that their power isn’t so super.”
Recent years have made it clear that “military power alone cannot secure peace,” he said.
Click on the player below for his full speech.
Trump says he thinks US will make deal with Iran after Midterms
The US president tells the UN General Assembly that he believes Washington will make a deal with Iran right after mid-term elections are held in November.
"I believe we'll make a deal right after the election because it doesn't make sense for them not to. They're waiting to see how I do in the midterm election," Trump says.
Iran's Guards rejected US attempt to establish contact, Guards spokesman says
Iranian Revolutionary Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebi said on Tuesday that the United States had tried to establish contact with the Guards, but they had rebuffed the effort.
"The Americans have tried to contact us but we refuse any such contact. Our dealings with the enemy -- as long as they remain hostile -- are conducted solely through arms," said Mohebi, adding that diplomacy was handled by Iran's foreign ministry.
Trump calls on all nations to economically isolate Iran
The Islamic republic is "weak and desperate", the US president tells the UN General Assembly.
Iran 'toughened' conditions for ending war after US deal collapse, Guards spokesman says
Iranian Revolutionary Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebi said on Tuesday that Tehran had hardened its conditions for ending the war with the United States following the collapse of a June deal aimed at ending hostilities.
"They broke the agreement and committed another vicious act. We have therefore toughened our conditions," said Mohebi, adding that if the US persisted with this course, "they will only make things difficult for themselves".
He added that the US has "no choice" but to accept Iran's conditions.
Trump says deciding between deal or driving Iran 'into hell' in UN General Assembly speech
US President Donald Trump kicks off his speech at the United Nations General Assembly Tuesday by saying he has to choose whether to "annihilate" Iran if it fails to make a deal to end the Middle East war.
"Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?" Trump says.
Iran to 'intensify' response if US launches new attacks, Guards spokesman says
Iranian Revolutionary Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebi said on Tuesday that Tehran would "undoubtedly intensify" its response if the United States launched new attacks on the Islamic republic.
"If they act recklessly and history repeats itself, our resistance will undoubtedly intensify, bolstered by the experience we have gained. This time, we will not merely retaliate; we will adopt an offensive posture, and America will come to regret its actions, suffering greater humiliation than ever before," said Mohebi in an interview with AFP.
West Bank settlements raise ethnic cleansing 'specter', UN chief says
Expansion of Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are damaging the prospect of peace between the Israelis and Palestinians while raising the "specter of ethnic cleansing", UN chief Antonio Guterres warned on Tuesday.
"Violence, displacement and settlement expansion by Israel in the Occupied West Bank are bulldozing the path to peace and raising the specter of ethnic cleansing. We cannot allow the two-state solution to disappear before our eyes," he said while opening the UN's signature diplomatic gathering.
Saudi King Salman condemns Houthis as 'terrorist militia' in rare statement
The king of Saudi Arabia denounced Yemen's Houthis as a "terrorist militia" in a rare statement reacting to an attack that authorities said targeted the holy city of Mecca last week.
King Salman, 90, praised the armed forces and security services for defending the country, and condemned the recent Houthi attempt "to target Mecca", calling it "a provocation to Muslims around the world", according to the official Saudi news agency.
Putin and Saudi Arabia's Mohammed bin Salman talk about need to keep key sea lanes open, Kremlin says
Russian President Vladimir Putin held a phone call with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in which they discussed the security situation in the Gulf and the need to keep vital waterways open, the Kremlin said.
It said the two leaders held a detailed exchange of views on the situation in the Middle East and emphasised that a political and diplomatic settlement remains the only viable path forward.
They also "underscored the need for a swift cessation of hostilities" in Yemen amid the deteriorating military and political situation there.
"The importance of ensuring the safe and unimpeded passage of vessels through the region's international waterways, including the Bab el-Mandeb and Strait of Hormuz, was emphasised," the Kremlin said.
Houthis say Saudi attack on Yemen prison kills at least nine
An attack by Saudi Arabia on a prison in northwestern Yemen killed at least nine detainees, a Houthi official told the Saba news agency, which is affiliated with the Iran-backed group.
"Nine prisoners captured during recent events were killed last night when the Saudi enemy targeted a prison" in Al-Hazm, in Al-Jawf governorate, said Houthi official Abdelkader al-Murtada.
More than 10,000 could flee Yemen fighting to Djibouti in coming months, says UN
Renewed fighting in Yemen could see the number of refugees fleeing across the Red Sea to Djibouti jump from 3,000 today to 10,000 in coming months, the United Nations warned.
The UN refugee agency is "planning for more than 10,000 arrivals in Djibouti", spokesman Babar Baloch told reporters in Geneva, adding that the number of people displaced within Yemen by the recent fighting could swell from more than 130,000 today to over 230,000 in coming months.
A displaced Yemeni cooks at Al-Firdaws camp in Ras Imran, on the western outskirts of Aden, Yemen, September 21, 2026. © Abdulnasser Alseddik, AP
Houthis say Saudi Arabia conducts deadly strike on key port city
Yemen's Houthis said Saudi Arabia carried out a deadly strike on a key port city on Tuesday, over a week into the Houthi offensive that has seen them seize control of a strait that is crucial to global energy flows.
G7 nations called on the Houthis meanwhile to halt cross-border strikes on Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen's internationally recognised government.
The Houthis' takeover of the country's Red Sea coast in a dramatic offensive that has left hundreds of people on both sides dead, has also threatened global trade and pushed up energy prices.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters, AP and AFP)
Yesterday's key developments:
-  Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi arrived in New York, leading Tehran's diplomatic delegation at the annual gathering of world leaders at the United Nations.
-  G7 foreign ministers called on Iran to end its arming and support of Houthis in Yemen, which they said constituted a dangerous pattern of escalation that risked undermining international trade and creating global instability.
-  Iran's Revolutionary Guard warned that it would “change the geography of the war” if the United States escalates the conflict.

articles.title: Russia strikes Ukraine industrial sites, killing 4, officials say
articles.body:
Russia strikes Ukraine industrial sites, killing 4, officials say
- Russia struck Ukraine's industrial cities Dnipro, Kryvyi Rih, and Pavlohrad, killing four and damaging businesses and infrastructure, using missiles, drones, and artillery.
- A Russian attack cut power to nearly 100,000 people in northern Ukraine's Chernihiv region and hit energy and port facilities in Poltava.
- Ukraine responded with drone attacks on Russian civilian targets, killing one in Samara, while Russia claimed to have destroyed 297 drones overnight.
AI generated
Russia hit Ukraine’s industrial heartland overnight, killing four, while an attack in the north cut power supply to thousands, Ukrainian officials said on Sept 22.
Moscow has escalated its air war, striking economic targets from businesses to logistics hubs as front-line fighting has largely stalled more than 4½ years into the war triggered by Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Both sides deny targeting civilians in the conflict.
Strikes on industrial cities
Moscow simultaneously hit industrial enterprises in the cities of Dnipro, Kryvyi Rih and Pavlohrad in the south-eastern region of Dnipropetrovsk, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said on the Telegram messaging app.
The region is home to machine building, steel-making and other major production.
Russia deployed missiles, drones and artillery at four districts, killing four people and injuring six in Dnipro, where Hanzha said that a business and warehouse premises were badly damaged.
The Russian barrage included an unspecified number of Oniks anti-ship and ballistic missiles, as well as four cruise missiles and 212 drones, Ukraine’s air force said.
Russia’s defence ministry said its forces hit industrial and military facilities in Ukraine, targeting the fuel and energy sector as well as port infrastructure facilities and sea vessels serving the Ukrainian military.
Businesses have also been damaged in Pavlohrad and Kryvyi Rih, the home town of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, Hanzha added.
A Russian attack on an energy facility in a neighbouring region cut power supplies to nearly 100,000 consumers in the northern region of Chernihiv, an electricity distributor said.
Moscow hit an industrial enterprise and a critical infrastructure facility in a “massive” attack on the central region of Poltava, Governor Vitalii Diakivnych said, without providing details.
Russia’s defence ministry said its forces hit an oil refinery in the city of Kremenchuk in the Poltava region.
Ukraine, in turn, has stepped up attacks on Russia, targeting the largest online retailers and oil refineries, often deep in the country’s territory.
Ukrainian drones hit civilian targets in Russia’s Samara region on the Volga River, the local governor said, killing one and injuring four. The region is home to critically important facilities, such as oil refineries.
The Russian defence ministry said air defence units destroyed 297 drones over various Russian regions overnight. REUTERS

articles.title: Saudi Arabia turns to Israel as Houthi attacks expose limits of the Mecca Pact - opinion
articles.body:
On August 7, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed a joint defense agreement, known as the Mecca Pact. At its public core is a political commitment modeled in part on NATO’s Article 5 – namely, an armed attack on one party is to be regarded as an attack on all.
On September 8, the Houthis launched a major wave of attacks against Saudi Arabia, striking civilian and economic sites and energy infrastructure in several southern cities. Subsequently, the country has been attacked time and again by the Houthis. Civilian and economic facilities have been struck; King Khalid Air Base and Aramco facilities have been targeted.
Why have Turkey and Pakistan not rushed to Saudi’s defense?
Rather like the small print on insurance policies, the Mecca Pact seems to exclude as much as it offers. The publicly released description of the agreement, while making much of the NATO-like commitment, does not specify an automatic military response should one of the parties be attacked. Nor does it publicly stipulate the circumstances in which troops must be deployed. In fact, the full text of the agreement has not been released, so important questions about its scope and implementation remain obscure.
Rather late in the day, on Saturday, Lt. Gen. Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, chief spokesman for Pakistan’s military, is reported as saying, “Pakistan fully stands with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, both diplomatically and physically…We will go to any extent.”
But the statement, whatever it meant, was too late. Given the ambiguities inherent in the Mecca Pact, and the obvious reluctance of either Pakistan or Turkey to become involved in a military operation in Yemen, it is not surprising that Saudi Arabia turned to Washington for support that subsequently connected it to Israel.
CENTCOM is the US military command responsible for the Middle East and parts of Central and South Asia. It directs US military operations and security partnerships in that area.
Sometime during the week of September 7, at a secluded ski resort in Germany (rumored to be Garmisch-Partenkirchen), CENTCOM’s commander, Admiral Brad Cooper, hosted a conference of senior military leaders from eight countries.
It is extraordinary, but the fact that sitting round the same table were Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, the IDF chief of staff, and military chiefs from Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt. CENTCOM, functioning as an intermediary, had succeeded in connecting Israel with Arab militaries that do not have diplomatic relations with it – in particular, Saudi Arabia and Qatar.
According to a report by Axios, the respected digital news outlet, the central purpose of the conference was to discuss the continuing US-Israeli war with Iran, and the broader regional-security situation.
Cooper reportedly assured those present that, despite Iranian attacks on US bases, the US would retain forces in the Middle East. He also primed the group on plans to expand maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
Zamir is said to have briefed the participants on IDF operations on several fronts.
Axios further reports, citing “a source with knowledge of the matter,” that Israel and Saudi Arabia, with CENTCOM assistance, began discussing how Israel could assist Saudi military operations against the Houthis. The possible support mentioned is ISR (intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance), on the lines of the assistance that Israel has reportedly provided to the UAE.
US agrees to assist Saudi Arabia
On September 14, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman met Cooper in Jeddah, amid the rapidly worsening Houthi offensive. The next day Reuters reported that Washington, while declining to conduct direct US strikes against the Houthis, had agreed to provide Saudi Arabia with targeted assistance.
That same day, September 15, The Jerusalem Post reported that Israel and Saudi Arabia had held CENTCOM-mediated discussions about Israeli intelligence assistance to Riyadh against the Houthis. Regional diplomatic sources had told the paper that the Saudi side was seeking intelligence that could help build a picture of Houthi deployments, and thus anticipate future operations.
A similar report emanated from the Institute for the Study of War in a document published jointly with the Critical Threats Project at the American Enterprise Institute. It commented that this prospective arrangement would: “…resemble Israel’s current intelligence support relationship with the United Arab Emirates.”
There is no doubt that the Iran war is creating an unusually powerful common-security denominator. The countries represented in CENTCOM’s conference have very different political relationships with Israel, but they share an immediate security problem: Iran. Iranian-aligned armed groups have acted against some of them and are capable of threatening all.
Israel possesses substantial intelligence and surveillance capabilities concerning Iran and its regional partners. Saudi’s cities and energy infrastructure have been struck repeatedly by Houthi missiles and drones. CENTCOM possesses the command-and-control machinery that can connect Israel and Saudi Arabia.
Although Saudi Arabia still has no formal diplomatic relations with Israel, the emerging arrangement potentially constitutes a major step in Saudi-Israeli military normalization. Israeli intelligence is being used to help defend Saudi Arabia against the Houthis, even without diplomatic normalization.
This arrangement gives Saudi Arabia considerable political cover. Publicly, its relationship with Israel can remain highly constrained; operationally, cooperation can become increasingly sophisticated.
So the present position, according to media reports, is that Saudi Arabia is being offered direct targeted support by the US, while CENTCOM is mediating Saudi-Israeli discussions on intelligence assistance against the Houthis.
Saudi-Israeli collaboration is nothing new. There is a 60-year history of covert strategic cooperation. But the Saudi-Israel connection remains as delicate as it has ever been. It is not any form of military alliance, nor has there been any change in Saudi policy on formal normalization. In fact, reports emanating from Saudi sources suggest that Riyadh, even while seeking Israel’s help against Houthi attacks, is still resisting movement on normalization.
Meanwhile, the law of unintended consequences is in full play. While the Houthis continue their strikes on Saudi Arabia and make territorial gains in areas surrounding one of the world’s critical maritime choke points, the Bab el-Mandeb, they are inadvertently fostering greater military cooperation than ever before between Israel and Arab states, and both reviving and strengthening Israel’s covert security links with Saudi Arabia.
The writer, a former senior civil servant, is the Middle East correspondent for Eurasia Review. Follow him at: www.a-mid-east-journal.blogspot.com.

articles.title: How Arab-Israeli air defense coordination is developing into a regional security shield - analysis
articles.body:
Operation Epic Fury helped improve coordination among US partners and allies in the region on air defenses and other areas. A recent Lead Inspector General Report to the United States Congress, which covers operations of Epic Fury from April to June, provided new details on the types of cooperation. Although the report is general, it sheds light on an important trend in the Middle East.
The report says that “US forces embedded in partner air operations centers across the region, which supported coordination, deconfliction, and synchronization of air defense efforts.”
It also discusses a Middle East Defense network, “an integrated missile defense architecture in the region - intercepted more than 6,000 OWUAS and more than 1,500 ballistic missiles that targeted US and partner forces.”
In addition, the report discusses how the US partnered with Israel. “Coordinated air and missile defense with Israel was also substantial, with US Patriot and THAAD systems operating alongside Israeli Arrow, David’s Sling, and Iron Dome systems. The United States and Israel maintained shared awareness and recurring reporting on readiness and intercept activity via embedded liaison officers in the Israeli military headquarters in Tel Aviv, known as HaKirya.”
The origins of this unprecedented cooperation grew out of foundations laid over the past few years. These include US Central Command (CENTCOM coordinating with Gulf partners and also with Israel.
Increasing cooperation throughout the Middle East
Over the last decade, Israel and CENTCOM have increasingly cooperated. This resulted in Israel moving from being under US European Command to being in CENTCOM's area of operations. The Abraham Accords paved the way for this move because it meant Israel could not work more openly with Gulf partners. In the past, Arab countries had generally refrained from any joint exercises with Israel. This made coordination difficult, even if it occurred quietly.
Much has changed in the Middle East in the last decade. In the wake of the 2015 Iran deal, Tehran increased its role in Yemen, Iraq, Syria and Lebanon. At the same time, countries in the region had to deal with ISIS threats that only began to decline after 2017.
Turkey’s hostile attitude to Egypt, Saudi Arabia and the UAE shifted considerably after 2019. Other trends began to change as well. Israel, Greece and Cyprus became closer partners. While COVID reduced joint exercises, Israel, the US, and other countries still had many opportunities to train together using advanced platforms such as the F-35.
After the Abraham Accords, there was increasing discussion about how Israel might integrate with the Gulf countries to coordinate defenses. Some saw a potential Middle Eastern defense pact, or a kind of regional NATO. That would require Saudi Arabia to normalize ties with Israel. Normalization didn’t happen.
Nevertheless, in January 2022, the Jewish Institute for National Security of America (JINSA) published a report called A Stronger and Wider Peace: A US Strategy for Advancing the Abraham Accords.
“The report heralded the Accords as an historic breakthrough and urged the US government to seize the opportunity to start building a new Middle East defense architecture premised on bringing America’s regional partners together in common cause to counter the growing menace from Iran.”
The goal was also for Congress to help support this cooperation and support a “region-wide air defense network to help deter and defeat the escalating missile and drone threat posed by Iran and its terrorist proxies.”
The result was the Deterring Enemy Forces and Enabling National Defenses Act (DEFEND Act) of 2022.
JINSA noted in a May 2023 report called “Build it, and they will come: A US strategy for integrating Middle East air and missile defenses,” that there were opportunities to move toward a “region-wide integrated air and missile defense (IAMD).”
JINSA noted that “animosities among US partners have historically acted as a severe constraint on their willingness to engage in the levels of intelligence sharing and cooperation that meaningful air defense integration would require.” The opportunities in 2023 were clear. Israel could work with the US and Gulf partners.
Hamas, Iran, Houthi attacks shifting sands of Middle Eastern relations
The October 7 Hamas attack was a setback to this regional integration. Iran wanted it to be a setback, and in some ways Tehran initially got its wish. Israel had to wage a grueling, long war in Gaza and then in Lebanon. The Houthis attacked Israel. Iran also carried out large direct attacks using hundreds of ballistic missiles.
The Iranian attacks and the Houthi attacks led to close cooperation between the US, Israel, and also regional partners against the ballistic missile and drone threat. This laid the foundations for what came next in 2025 and 2026.
The full extent of cooperation during Epic Fury is yet to be revealed. Nevertheless, the fact that air defense systems, such as THAAD, Patriots, and Israel’s David’s Sling, Arrow, and Iron Dome, were able to work together is important.
The US is also selling more defense systems to the Gulf. As the Gulf countries modernize their systems, more opportunities for joint cooperation will occur. In addition, there will be more chances for joint exercises and drills in the future.
The tempo of war since 2023 has largely pushed off some of these drills. It remains to be seen if Saudi Arabia will acquire the F-35. If it does, it would join Israel and CENTCOM as an operator of the 5th-generation warplane over the next decade.
The recent Lead Inspector General Report sheds light on how Iran targets countries in the region. It also shows how the US has “been helping grow the sovereign military defense of Gulf partners for decades to counter Iranian attacks and safeguard regional stability. This has included the provision of military sales, training, and information-sharing to Gulf partners.”
This is all good news. The fact that such a large number of 6,000 drone attacks and 1,500 ballistic missile attacks were intercepted further illustrates the success.
Iran has hinted that it is developing new threats. The learning curve has already shown that Israel and other countries in the region are prepared for many of these threats.
Nevertheless, the war will result in some changes. There is talk of the US shifting away from some bases in the Gulf. This could mean more deployment in Jordan or in Israel.
CENTCOM will be learning many lessons alongside Israel regarding what comes next.

articles.title: Iran, US diplomatic signals raise hopes for renewed peace talks
articles.body:
Senior Iran and United States officials made diplomatic overtures Tuesday, raising hopes for a renewed talks to the Middle East conflict.
A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran could reopen the Strait of Hormuz to Gulf shipping within days if the U.S. lifts its blockade, describing a gathering at the U.N. as a "golden opportunity" to renew diplomacy with Washington.
U.S. President Donald Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian are both due to attend the U.N. General Assembly in New York, the first time they will be at the same event since Trump launched "Operation Epic Fury" against Iran in February.
The Iranian official said Iran's delegation had full authority to revive talks, although no direct meetings between the two presidents were planned.
No face-to-face meetings between Iran and the United States are known to have taken place since July, when an agreement on an interim deal to end the war collapsed just weeks after it was signed by Trump and Pezeshkian.
"The U.S. needs to announce that it wants to resolve the issue diplomatically, make that official and then agree on a timeline for how the process will move forward," the Iranian official said.
"The U.N. General Assembly is a golden opportunity for the U.S. to return to diplomacy," the official said. He said Iran had sent its latest proposal to Washington via mediators on Sept. 16.
Meanwhile, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told NBC's "Today" show the U.S. was open to speaking with the Iranians at the General Assembly.
"We're open to that. I don't think anything is scheduled at this point, but we're certainly open to something like that, especially if it has the prospects of leading to something positive and ultimately achieving the goal of what this is all about," Rubio said.
"And that is the fact that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon. They just simply can't."
Trump is due to meet Tuesday with the leaders of the six Gulf Arab states: Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
The Gulf countries are keen to restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz but wary of giving their longstanding rival Iran too much power.
All apart from Oman host huge U.S. military bases that have come under repeated Iranian attack throughout the war, which has strained their decades-old security partnerships with Washington.
The biggest of them, Saudi Arabia, has been drawn deeper into the war this month, with Iran-backed Houthi rebels advancing in Yemen, routing forces of a Saudi-backed government there and threatening Saudi oil exports through the Red Sea.
There was some relief on oil markets Tuesday, after sources told Reuters that Saudi Arabia had restarted operations at its East-West Pipeline and could resume exports within hours, albeit at reduced volume, from the Red Sea port of Yanbu.
The pipeline, Saudi Arabia's main alternative route for exports to bypass wartime disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, was shut down after attacks on Sept. 10 that Riyadh blamed on Iranian allies in Iraq.
The Houthis have pushed back Saudi-supported government forces with the aim of controlling the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the southern mouth of the Red Sea and have attacked Saudi Arabia directly with missiles and drones.
The U.S., which bombed the Houthis for two months last year, has so far rebuffed repeated pleas from Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to rejoin the fight against the group.
The New York Times reported that Trump called off U.S. strikes against the Houthis Sunday at the last minute, after troops had already begun loading bombs onto planes.
On the table at the Gulf states' meeting with Trump is a Qatari proposal for a framework to bring Iran and the Arab Gulf states into a common security architecture, regional sources said.
Speaking at a Qatar Economic Forum in New York on Sunday, Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani said any such arrangement would need to provide security guarantees for the Gulf states and expand economic interdependence with Iran.
"Lasting security cannot be built through repeated cycles of escalations and retaliation, or arrangements that leave any state permanently exposed to insecurity," Sheikh Mohammed said.
Another source in the region told Reuters Iran was reviewing the proposal.
Houthi fighters in Yemen are pushing to seize the strategic heights of the Kahboub Mountains to cut off the Red Sea coast from remaining areas held by Saudi-backed forces.
The area of Kahboub overlooks the western coastline and Bab el-Mandeb, and would provide a commanding position from which the Houthis could seek to exert greater control over both.
Its rugged landscape also makes it easier for Houthi fighters to remain concealed from drones and air strikes than on the coastal plain.
The fighting has already displaced more than 130,000 people this month and the U.N. refugee agency said Tuesday that tens of thousands more people could be driven from their homes.

articles.title: Danish defense startup guarding undersea cables runs on 15 Ukrainian suppliers. Ukrainian fund is putting in €2 million in it
articles.body:
A Ukrainian fund is investing in a Danish defense startup, a reversal for a country far better known for taking in foreign capital than for sending it abroad. Resist.UA is backing BlueShadow, a maritime security firm run by a former US Navy submarine commander but largely engineered in Ukraine, to build defenses for coasts and undersea cables against drones and hybrid attacks.
BlueShadow is registered in Denmark, but almost its entire engineering team works in Ukraine, and it folds gear from more than 15 Ukrainian suppliers of drones, sensors, and communications into a single system.
Resist.UA, which signed a letter of intent to join the company's €2 million pre-seed round, runs a new €50 million fund, Resist 2.0, designed to bring Ukraine's battlefield-proven technology to global markets.
Ukraine engineers the Danish startup
The company was founded in 2025 and is led by Charles Maher, a former commander of a US Navy nuclear submarine, according to Defender Media.
This summer, it registered as a Ukrainian legal entity and builds on Ukrainian components, planning to fit its maritime platforms with M-Fly's RB-220 gimbal, a day-and-night targeting sensor used until now only on flying drones.
The two sides first met in January 2026 and formalized the partnership as BlueShadow raised its round and Resist.UA launched its second fund.
The systems guard the sea
BlueShadow is building two of them. BlueDragon, still in development, is designed to shield Ukraine's coastal cities, ports, and shipping lanes from drone strikes. BlueSentry, which the company plans to launch in October, is aimed at protecting ports, offshore wind farms, undersea cables, and maritime borders from hybrid attack, the kind of sabotage that has repeatedly damaged Baltic Sea infrastructure.
"This partnership will fuel the next phase of our mission to protect people, infrastructure, commerce, and natural resources at sea," the company said.
Ukraine's defense tech turns outward
Ukrainian defense technology, tested in real combat, has drawn growing investor interest, and Ukrainian figures are now building funds to channel it: the former Defense Minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, is raising what he calls the country's largest defense-tech venture fund.
