articles.title: Iran ready to reopen Hormuz within 7 days if US eases pressure
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran ready to reopen Strait of Hormuz within 7 days if US eases military pressure and lifts blockade
Iran can reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if the United States eases military pressure and lifts its blockade on Iranian ports, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Tuesday.
On Sunday, Iran's military central command said it was informed the US was preparing to restart military operations with the support of regional countries, and warned this would lead to Tehran's retaliation "without limitations and considerations".
"The US needs to announce that it wants to resolve the issue diplomatically, make that official, and then agree on a timeline for how the process will move forward", the senior Iranian official said, adding the Iranian delegation to the United Nations General Assembly is in New York and has full authority to revive diplomacy with the United States.
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, who left Tehran for New York on Tuesday morning, will not meet US President Donald Trump at the UN headquarters in New York, the official told Reuters.
The Iranian official said details on an agreement to end hostilities with Washington can be discussed in New York via mediators, explaining that Tehran's proposal was delivered to the US via mediators on 16 September.
"The UN General Assembly is a golden opportunity for the US to return to diplomacy", the official said, adding that Tehran would welcome a revival of diplomacy if Washington takes tangible steps.
Meanwhile, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday the US is open to speaking with Iranians at the UN General Assembly, but no meeting is currently scheduled.
"We're open to that. I don't think anything is scheduled at this point, but we're certainly open to something like that, especially if it has the prospects of leading to something positive and ultimately achieving the goal of what this is all about," Rubio said in an interview with NBC's "Today" show.
"And that is the fact that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon. They just simply can't," he insisted.
Both the United States and Israel—who jointly launched a war on Iran at the end of February—possess nuclear weapons.

articles.title: Lithuania’s Seimas backs move to remove constitutional ban on nuclear weapons
articles.body:
Lithuania’s parliament on Tuesday backed a proposal to remove from the constitution a ban on stationing weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases on the country’s territory, opening the way for a potential future deployment of NATO nuclear weapons.
The proposal received 99 votes in favour, 13 against and five abstentions during its consideration in the Seimas. The vote advances the constitutional amendment but does not itself authorise the deployment of nuclear weapons in Lithuania.
The Constitution’s Article 137 currently states that weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases may not be stationed on Lithuanian territory.
Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said the first vote on adopting the constitutional amendment is scheduled for October 6, with the final vote planned for January 12, 2027.
Constitutional amendments require two votes separated by at least three months, with at least 94 of the 141 lawmakers required to approve the measure at each final stage.
Remigijus Žemaitaitis, leader of the Nemunas Dawn party, opposed the proposal, arguing that Russia and Belarus could use it for propaganda purposes. He also said nuclear-armed states would be able to use nuclear weapons to defend Lithuania if necessary without removing the constitutional provision.
He argued that the relevant constitutional article should only be changed through a referendum.
Ignas Vėgėlė, a member of the parliament’s mixed group, questioned why the proposal would remove the entire provision rather than only the restriction on weapons of mass destruction. The article also prohibits foreign military bases.
“Why are we deleting this part of the sentence as well? Are we planning to hand over Lithuanian territory to military bases that we will not control or manage?” Vėgėlė asked.
He noted that Lithuania’s Constitutional Court has ruled that allied foreign military bases can operate in Lithuania if they are established by allies and remain under Lithuanian control. He argued that a similar principle should apply to weapons of mass destruction.
Laurynas Kasčiūnas, parliamentary leader of the opposition Homeland Union-Lithuanian Christian Democrats, said nuclear weapons are a key component of deterrence.
He said nuclear deterrence helped prevent the Cold War from becoming a direct military conflict and argued that Lithuania should not maintain restrictions that do not apply to some of its NATO allies.
“We are the only country in the region that has this restriction. Latvia does not have it, Estonia does not have it, Poland does not have it, Finland has just removed it,” Kasčiūnas said.
He cited a hypothetical scenario in which a US allied ship carrying nuclear weapons or a nuclear-capable aircraft might need to pass through Lithuanian territory for deterrence purposes.
Kasčiūnas stressed that removing the ban would not mean Lithuania had decided to station nuclear weapons there, but said eliminating the constitutional restriction would give the country more options as part of NATO’s deterrence arrangements.
Remigijus Motuzas, chairman of the Seimas Foreign Affairs Committee and a Social Democrat, also said Lithuania should not create obstacles to NATO’s nuclear deterrence or become the weaker link in the alliance’s regional security posture.
“Lithuania must clearly show our allies and adversaries that we will defend our independence by all means,” Motuzas said. “We cannot be less protected than other NATO countries.”
He said changing the constitution would send a strong signal intended to reduce the risk of military aggression.
Liberal Movement leader Viktorija Čmilytė-Nielsen said deterrence should not be viewed as an escalation of war.
“Today’s vote is about ensuring that we are not weaker,” she said.
The proposal comes amid broader discussions in Europe about nuclear deterrence. French President Emmanuel Macron has promoted the idea of developing a European nuclear deterrence framework under which partner countries could potentially host French strategic aircraft equipped with nuclear weapons.
The Financial Times reported in June that the United States was considering deploying nuclear weapons in additional NATO countries in Europe, although no such deployment in Lithuania has been announced.

articles.title: Zelenskyy began meetings in New York — whom he met with and what they discussed
articles.body:
Zelenskyy began meetings in New York — whom he met with and what they discussed
Kyiv • UNN
Zelenskyy met with U.S. senators and Macron before talks with Trump. They discussed sanctions against the russian federation, de-escalation, and Ukraine’s air defense needs.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy began meetings in New York on September 22 as part of his visit to the United States, where he is expected to meet with President of the United States Donald Trump, UNN reports.
The head of state has already held talks with American lawmakers and French President Emmanuel Macron. The sides discussed sanctions against russia, de-escalation, and air defense.
Meeting with U.S. senators
He began his visit to New York with a meeting with U.S. senators. I thanked them for their strong bipartisan support for Ukraine and for voting in favor of Lindsey Graham’s sanctions bill. A very important step. And when it is fully implemented, peace and guaranteed security will definitely be closer. We agreed that our teams would work more closely on sanctions
The president said that he told the senators about "proposals for de-escalation that we will discuss with the President of America."
"We also discussed our needs for ballistic interceptors and the challenges ahead of winter. There are things we can do together with America to protect lives. It is currently impossible to replace American "Patriots," and the more anti-ballistic protection Ukraine has, the less audacity russia will have to continue its strikes and prolong the war. Thank you!" Zelenskyy stated.
Talks with Macron
President Zelenskyy also met with his French counterpart Macron.
"I met with Emmanuel Macron. We spoke primarily about security and the winter support package for Ukraine. We are also ready to provide additional SAMP/T air defense systems and missiles for them using financial resources within the framework of the EU loan," Zelenskyy noted.

articles.title: World leaders gather at UN amid wars, AI fears and global divisions
articles.body:
World leaders gather at UN amid wars, AI fears and global divisions
World leaders are gathering at the United Nations this week against a backdrop of wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, rising fears over artificial intelligence and mounting economic and climate pressures. The annual General Assembly will test whether the 193-member body can still bring countries together to tackle crises that increasingly transcend borders.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Under a global cloud of wars and bitter divisions, world leaders meet at the United Nations this week facing new fears that runaway artificial intelligence could threaten humanity even as climate shocks and escalating prices are already making life much tougher for hundreds of millions of people.
The annual high-level gathering at the UN General Assembly will also be consumed with major wars in Iran , Gaza , Ukraine, Sudan , Congo and Myanmar and a persisting question: Can the leaders do anything to end them?
And what can they do about the relentless rise of global warming threatening the future of the planet, the growing inequalities within and among nations, and shocks to the global economy as blocked shipping routes and supply chains increase the cost of living and slow growth?
The future of the United Nations will also definitely be on the agenda. At 81, its powers are still the victorious nations from World War II, not the 21st century’s major global players. The UN’s 193 member nations have agreed to a wide-ranging reform package that includes updating key institutions such as the powerful UN Security Council, where the US, Russia, China, Britain and France hold inordinate sway because of their veto power. Reform, however, is easier said than implemented.
Read moreMacron says talks with Trump on Ukraine, Red Sea were 'constructive'
Behind the scenes, there will be speculation about who will lead the United Nations next. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres’ second five-year term ends Dec. 31 and no clear successor has emerged.
This meeting is still pivotal
There is still no question that the UN remains THE gathering place for its 193 member nations and their leaders. Some 130 heads of state and government are expected to speak at the General Assembly starting Tuesday along with dozens of ministers.
Among the headliners will be US President Donald Trump and French President Emanuel Macron. Both will speak Tuesday after Guterres’ opening “state of the world” address. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky and Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian speak Wednesday.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu — whom New York Mayor Zoran Mamdani wanted arrested for his treatment of Palestinians in Gaza until he learned he has no such authority — will address the assembly on Thursday. For a second year, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas won’t be coming to the UN because the U.S. has refused to give him a visa. He will nonetheless address the assembly by video the same day.
The United States, under its agreement with the UN to host the organisation, is required to allow diplomats from all member nations to attend meetings.
Equally telling is who else isn’t coming. China’s President Xi Jinping is meeting Trump in Washington on Wednesday, yet he is skipping – some diplomats say snubbing – the UN gathering and sending a vice president instead. Russian President Vladimir Putin isn’t coming either, and Indian President Narendra Modi has backed out.
France's UN ambassador, Jérôme Bonnafont, said it is “extremely critical” for world leaders this week to support the UN as the place where the world’s nations meet – especially at a time of such polarisation.
“We believe in multilateralism," he said, "and we believe that the high-level week is the occasion for countries in the world to reaffirm that they prefer cooperation and dialogue to confrontation.”
United Nations has not had a great year
There is no doubt it’s been a tough year for the world body. It has been pushed to the sidelines when it comes to its key responsibility of ensuring international peace and security and trying to end major conflicts in the Mideast and Ukraine. The US failure to pay billions of dollars in outstanding arrears has left the organization’s finances in rocky shape.
But veteran UN watcher Richard Gowan, the International Crisis Group’s global issues and institutions program director, says 2025 was even worse.
A year ago, he said, people were contemplating that Trump would use his UN speech to announce that the United States would leave the world organization. Trump didn’t announce a pullout last September and the UN muddled through the past 12 months with financial troubles that forced cutbacks to its peacekeeping operations and humanitarian aid.
In recent days, the US paid $725 million of its dues to the UN’s regular operating budget for this year, enough to keep the Trump administration from losing its vote in the General Assembly. The payment was a strong indication Trump will keep the US in the United Nations.
The UN is no longer “in freefall”, Gowan said, but it “is stuck in an open-ended or permanent crisis”. Put more graphically, he said, “The UN may not be in emergency care like it was last year, but it does seem to be trapped in a trauma centre for the foreseeable future.”
Former UN deputy secretary-general Mark Malloch-Brown, a United Nations Foundation board member, said, “While the world still trusts the UN, the global public is eager for change."
AI is pushing toward the centre of the agenda
The future of artificial intelligence has pushed to the forefront of global concerns, with its speeding advances and the dawning recognition that there are no industry controls, let alone any global guardrails for a technology that has many advantages but also many disadvantages and unknowns.
WatchAI-pocalypse? Tech leaders, politicians clash over development slowdown
Days before the global gathering, leaders of three major AI companies warned about the technology getting out of human control and called for a pause, but Trump dismissed their concerns as “a hoax”, and urged continued advances to keep the US ahead of China.
The UN Security Council added a high-level meeting on AI to its agenda on Wednesday afternoon, a sign of the growing apprehension and need to address the issue. It was already slated to hold a high-level meeting on Ukraine with Zelensky on Wednesday morning.
For the UN chief, this will be his last assembly meeting with global leaders. He previewed his speech last week, telling UN reporters that power is shifting in “an era of deep uncertainty".
“At a time when the world faces three existential threats," he said, “international cooperation is more necessary than ever.”
Others will be vying for the spotlight on issues from rising sea levels and funding education to the fight for gender equality. Hundreds of private meetings will also convene in UN cubicles, hotels, diplomatic missions and restaurants.
Esther Brimmer, a senior fellow in global governance at the Council on Foreign Relations and former US assistant secretary of state for international organization affairs in the Obama administration, said in-person meetings can help countries hash out ideas that get implemented months later.
She called the situation in 2026 “much more serious and complex than in decades past".
“With that said, I’m also not without hope as well,” Brimmer said. “Over the past decades we’ve learned a lot about international cooperation.”
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

articles.title: Davey says far right in Britain now better funded and supported than in the past – UK politics live
articles.body:
Trump says his relationship with UK better now with Burnham as PM than with Starmer
Donald Trump was being polite and respectful for most of the very short press conference he held with Andy Burnham, but towards the end he could not resist a jibe about Keir Starmer.
Asked about UK-US relations by a reporter who said they had gone up and down, Trump replied:
No I think they’re up.
Well they’re more up now than they were with your last prime minister, let me put it that way.
I think right now, based on my relationship with the prime minister, Andy, I think that, I think we’re doing very well.
At one point the relationship between Trump and Starmer was good. But it got worse as Starmer started to criticise Trump publicly on issues like his proposal to annex Greenland, and his claim British troops avoided frontline action in Afghanistan. And the full rupture came when Keir Starmer refused to allow the US to use British airbases for attacks against Iran at the start of the war.
Burnham defends sanctions on West Bank settlements, as Trump does not criticise and claims to be unaware of details
At the press conference, Andy Burnham also defended the decision to impose sanctions on the West Bank settlements.
A US reporter asked Donald Trump what he thought about this. Trump claimed that he did not know about this. He asked Burnham if he knew about it.
And Burnham replied:
Yes. Obviously we took that decision, the foreign secretary [Ed Miliband] and I. And we did call you just to say why we had taken that.
I take this view on this issue. We have all spoken the years about the importance of the two-state solution. If we face the situation where there is a tender on the West Bank that in effect make a two-state solution non-viable, what do we do? Because if we do nothing, then if further erodes people’s trust in politics, hey think you’re all talks, when it comes to it you are not prepared to follow up on that talk and do something.
Burnham said he condemned the Hamas attacks on 7 October “completely”.
But politicians had to show there was meaning behind their words, he said.
Trump backs Burnham after PM says he wants to give UK a 'positive story' and 'hopefulness'
In response to a question about whether he was happier in Manchester of Manhatten at the short, 12-minute press conference, Andy Burnham talked about the great city of Manchester and referred to Donald Trump once calling it a “town”. Burnham went on, jokingly: “We don’t, I don’t hold it against you, as the former mayor.”
Burnham said he loved the US too.
And he launched into a riff about patriotism.
I was explaining to the president today, Britain has been in too much turbulence, a sense of us not know where were are going. And I think you responded when I said we’re going to lay out a plan for Britain, 10-year direction.
The country’s got so much going for it. And it’s time to turn the story about Britain to a positive story, get some hopefulness going around the country.
And I think you were saying today that very much is how you see it.
Trump said he agreed. He said there was a tremendous patriotism about Britain. And he joked about it having “got more names than any other place in the world”, because some people called it Britain, and some the United Kingdom, and some England.
He said it was just “waiting for good leadership, waiting for success”.
'We've done a great job' - Trump defends his record in Iran
At the press conference the Guardian’s Pippa Crerar asked Donald Trump if he expected UK to help him if he chose to annihilate Iran. And she asked if he had any sympathy for the allies are suffering because of rising petrol prices due to the war.
Trump did not really engage with any of her points.
Instead, he gave quite a rambling answer, saying:
I think as soon as the war is over, the numbers are going to come way down, pricing generally.
Oil is the big thing when the oil goes up.
And we had to do that because we have to stop them. And I think we feel very united on that. We can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.
And people understand that in the United States, and they’re paying less than Biden, by the way, less than the Biden administration. And yet he did nothing about the threat of nuclear terror.
It’s nuclear terror. We can’t have it. So we’ve stopped them from having a nuclear weapon. We’ve literally stopped them. They’re not going to have a nuclear weapon. And we’ll see what happens.
I think that a settlement is going to be reached. They want to talk to us. They have been talking to us, even today. The relationship is developing, let’s say.
But we can’t let them … have a nuclear weapon. And there’s a price to pay for that.
This should have been done by other presidents. Or, frankly, other countries. Some country could have stepped forward. But there aren’t too many countries, frankly, that could have handled that.
So I think we’ve done a great job. They will not have a nuclear weapon.
Yesterday Andy Burnham spoke to the prime minister of Mauritius, Navin Ramgoolam, This is what Downing Street said in the readout of the call about what was said about the Chagos Islands deal.
Turning to the future of the military base on Diego Garcia, the prime minister underlined his commitment to working with Mauritius and the United States on a way forward that secures the operation of the base and protects UK national security.
And this is what Nigel Farage, who has been urging Donald Trump to block the Chagos Islands deal for about a year, posted on social media tonight after Trump’s comments. (See 6.20pm.)
Trump describes Chagos Islands deal as 'terrible', and claims Burnham has agreed to review it
Donald Trump described the Chagos Islands deal – a proposal by Keir Starmer’s goverment to give Mauritius sovereignty over the Chagos Islands, on condition that the US and the UK can continue to operate the Diego Garcia military base there for at least another 99 years – as “terrible”.
In the short press conference with Burnham, Trump said:
I don’t support it. I think it’s a terrible deal.
They all of a sudden say they have ownership, somebody has ownership that never showed up before after decades and centuries. I think it’s ridiculous. No, we were talking about that.
It’s strategically very important, very important. You know, we had to send our B-2 bombers when we bombed the Iran nuclear, we sent the B-2 bombers back home to Missouri. As opposed to flying for a short period of time, they had to fly for a long period of time.
It’s amazing how strategic it is, and I think the prime minister is going to be looking at it. It’s very strategic location. And it’s unique
It’s a very important piece of real estate, militarily and strategically.
Trump says his relationship with UK better now with Burnham as PM than with Starmer
Donald Trump was being polite and respectful for most of the very short press conference he held with Andy Burnham, but towards the end he could not resist a jibe about Keir Starmer.
Asked about UK-US relations by a reporter who said they had gone up and down, Trump replied:
No I think they’re up.
Well they’re more up now than they were with your last prime minister, let me put it that way.
I think right now, based on my relationship with the prime minister, Andy, I think that, I think we’re doing very well.
At one point the relationship between Trump and Starmer was good. But it got worse as Starmer started to criticise Trump publicly on issues like his proposal to annex Greenland, and his claim British troops avoided frontline action in Afghanistan. And the full rupture came when Keir Starmer refused to allow the US to use British airbases for attacks against Iran at the start of the war.
Trump says Burnham will be 'great PM', and Burnham says they have 'good connection', after friendly first meeting
At the start of the meeting with the press, this is what Donald Trump said about Andy Burnham.
I think he’s going to be a great prime minister. I think he’s got a lot of assets on his side.
We talked about everything from Rolls-Royce to energy, immigration. We covered a lot.
[The UK] is a really special country. And we are with you all the way, Mr Prime Minister.
And Burnham replied:
Thank you Mr President.
That’s wonderful. We really appreciate that.
This relationship matters so much to us. And we will build on that relationship.
You and I have established a good connection in our early discussions, and we’ve taken that further today.
We touched on Ukraine and it’s great to hear what you said today about the potential for progress there.
You know that we’re still ready to play our part in the Middle East in terms of helping you stop the conflict, open the strait [of Hormuz].
Obviously, we’re with you that Iran must never be a nuclear power.
We accepted a call from Saudi Arabia … we are prepared to play our part.
And obviously you were good enough today to let us talk about some issues on trade. The Falklands we mentioned. And you were good enough to listen to us on those issues.
So it has been great to be with you and the team today.
Burnham admits immigration big issue in UK politics
Burnham picks up on the topic of immigration. He says:
It was a very big issue at the Makerfield byelection and a lot of the British media will know that.
And I spoke about it then – our commitment is to get to a controlled approach. That’s what people want to see.
They’re not against migration overall. They know that people work in the NHS and in the care system. [There’s a] difference, though, when it’s managed or when it’s uncontrolled.
And the small boats is a very big issue for people. But crossings this summer were down 50% there or thereabouts on the number six years ago.
So sometimes people don’t hear that the progress is being made. But the progress is being made.
Trump adopts positive tone about Burnham, saying he's 'natural businessperson', after their first meeting
Donald Trump is talking.
He is referring to a “great election win”. It is not clear if he mean’s Labour’s in 2024, or Andy Burnham’s – in Makerfield.
Burnham thanks Trump for his remarks.
He says he thinks they have established a “good connection”.
The BBC’s Chris Mason asks Trump if Burnham is someone he can do business with.
Trump says he thinks he is.
He describes Burnham as a “natural businessperson”.
We’ve had a lot of discussions even before this meeting. We’ve spoken to each other numerous times on the phone. I think so, I think so. He gets it. He understands what he has to do.
(There are not many people who describe Burnham as a natural businessperson. He is a natural communciator, and a natural communicator and leader, but his experience of the business world is pretty limited. Maybe this was just Trump’s way of saying he liked him. Or maybe by “businessperson” he means ‘person you can do a deal with’. Still, it was positive.)
Originally journalists were told they would talk to the press briefly at the start of the meeting.
But now reporters have been told that they will be let in as the meeting ends for some words. Whether that will just be a few platitudes as Trump and Burnham pose for pictures, or whether they will take questions, is not entirely clear.
They are not in the Oval Office in the White House (which is looking even more lavish than usual now that Trump has given it billionaire bling decor). Instead they are at the United Nations building, which is functional and a bit shabby. Here is a shot from the live feed from the room where reporters are waiting.
We were told that the meeting would last for about half an hour, which means it should have been over by now. But nothing ever runs on time at the UN …

articles.title: Why are Hungary and Ukraine fighting again?
articles.body:
Why are Hungary and Ukraine fighting again?
After months of getting the diplomatic run-around from Kiev, Hungary has just backed out of Ukraine’s ‘Carpathian Eight’ initiative, leaving egg all over Vladimir Zelensky’s face, who only announced the group on Friday.
The first summit of the Carpathian Eight, where we launched the Carpathian Integration Initiative.
May the EU’s Carpathian macro-region remain strong. And may this format support us on our path to joining the European Union. I thank all the leaders of the C8 countries,… pic.twitter.com/sS4eojyiZx
Even with a pro-Kiev government in Budapest, the Ukrainians are discovering that politics is a two-way street.
The Carpathian Eight (C8) is a cooperation format aimed at tying Ukraine closer to seven of its neighbors: Austria, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, Romania, Serbia, and Slovakia. Under the Ukrainian-led initiative, these countries will cooperate on matters of security, energy, and trade.
What does Ukraine want from the Carpathian Eight?
Energy. Endemic corruption and neglect has left the country’s power grid unprotected against Russian missile and drone strikes as winter sets in. The initiative’s members want funding for 42 energy-related projects, 30 of which are located in Ukraine.
One project involves the construction of concrete shielding around oil tanks – a task that the Ukrainian state has already received EU money to complete. RT readers will remember that Vladimir Zelensky’s friend Timur Mindich skimmed some $100 million off Energoatom’s budget for doing just the same with its substations.
Another project – a gas turbine power plant in Ukraine’s Ivano-Frankivsk region – would see its backers transfer more than $1.2 billion to DTEK, an energy company run by a ‘former’ mafia enforcer that already received $112 million in EU and US aid in November 2024.
The group is also seeking cash to upgrade the Trans-Balkan Gas Corridor which Ukrainian Energy Minister Denis Shmigal has said would “significantly expand [Ukraine’s] access to diversified sources of natural gas supply,” and will help Kiev fill up its underground gas storage system.
The Carpathian Eight’s website lists a total of 123 investment projects costing $71.3 billion, across sectors including agriculture, manufacturing, and transport. Out of these, 86 are located in Ukraine.
The benefits to Ukraine are obvious, even if some of the Carpathian Eight’s contradictions appear unresolvable. Why, for instance, would anti-war Slovakia lobby for fortifying Ukraine’s energy grid, when Bratislava wants the conflict resolved peacefully above all else? And why would any of Ukraine’s neighbors back the initiative’s seven agriculture projects, all of which are located in Ukraine and stand to undercut Czech, Hungarian, Polish, Romanian, and Slovak farmers?
Did Zelensky jump the gun?
With so much to gain, it’s no surprise that Zelensky announced the Carpathian Eight as a done deal. However, neither Slovakia nor Hungary sent senior officials to the group’s inaugural meeting on Friday, and Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar pumped the brakes on the initiative on Monday.
“We were invited, and for good reasons we did not go,” Magyar said in parliament, stressing that Hungary “is not participating in this.” Magyar then announced that a proposed fuel storage facility for Ukraine on Hungarian soil would not go ahead as long as his government was in office.
Hungarian energy concern MOL and Ukraine’s Naftogaz signed off on the project on Sunday. According to Magyar, MOL did so without consulting the Hungarian government first.
How did the Ukrainians react?
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrey Sybiga took to social media to respond. “We are surprised by the Hungarian Prime Minister’s unnecessarily confrontational statements toward Ukraine,” he wrote on X on Tuesday. “What we’ve been hearing from Budapest lately leaves us confused. It seems that while Viktor Orban is gone, his policies of obstructionism and isolationism continue to thrive.”
“Orbanism has done no good, neither to Hungary nor to the broader region, in the past – and it will not do anyone any good moving forward,” Sybiga added.
I am helping you. To claim that a sovereign country is a member of an international cooperation (Carpathian Integration) without prior consultation or consent of the country concerned is completey unacxeptable. Just to give you an example: Hi, we have formed a football team in…
— Magyar Péter (Ne féljetek) (@magyarpeterMP) September 21, 2026
Magyar spelled out his problem in the replies. “I am helping you,” he wrote. “To claim that a sovereign country is a member of an international cooperation (Carpathian Integration) without prior consultation or consent of the country concerned is completely unacceptable.”
“Just to give you an example: Hi, we have formed a football team in the next village. We don’t know each other, but you are in it, and you have to bring the ball.”
What’s Hungary’s issue with Ukraine?
“You are in it, and you have to bring the ball” sums up the premise of the Carpathian Eight. The initiative’s members gain little from participation, save for becoming de-facto lobbyists for foreign investment in Ukraine. Sybiga’s indignation at the thought of a country rejecting this one-sided deal sums up the entitlement of the Ukrainian elite.
It’s the same entitlement displayed when Zelensky erupted in rage at the White House; when Sybiga’s predecessor, Dmitry Kuleba, berated the German government into handing over weapons; and when Kiev blew its EU-provided military budget on an “influence campaign” of long-range strikes before turning around and asking for more. Zelensky’s more recent demand that the EU not de-list Russian tycoons Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from its sanctions regime is a similar case of overreach.
Why have things turned so sour between Budapest and Kiev
The Zelensky/Magyar spat could have been easily avoided. After taking office in May, Magyar lifted Hungary’s veto on the EU’s €90 billion ($106 billion) loan package for Ukraine, dropped Orban’s blanket ban on EU accession talks with Kiev, and backed Brussels’ 20th package of anti-Russian sanctions.
All Zelensky had to do in exchange was guarantee the language rights of Ukraine’s Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia. Around 150,000 ethnic Hungarians live in the region, where a series of increasingly draconian language laws have banned the use of Hungarian in schools and public institutions. Despite losing their language rights, these ethnic Hungarians have still been subjected to Zelensky’s brutal military draft, provoking fierce condemnation from both Magyar and Viktor Orban’s governments.
Zelensky and Magyar reached what the Hungarian PM called a “formal agreement” to protect the rights of the Transcarpathian Hungarians in June. However, this agreement was strictly verbal. Anita Orban, Magyar’s foreign minister (and no relation of Viktor), has said that Zelensky agreed to an 11-point plan put forward by Budapest, but no document has emerged, and no legislative steps have been taken in Ukraine.
The historic agreement between Hungary and Ukraine on the educational, cultural, linguistic, and political rights of the Hungarian community in Transcarpathia has now been formalised.
In an formal diplomatic note, the Ukrainian side has committed itself to implementing all…
Zelensky’s promises, Magyar said at a press conference earlier this month, have “not yet been implemented.”
The takeaway
What Zelensky, Sybiga, and the rest of the Kiev regime have apparently yet to learn is that politics is a game of give and take. Magyar took office promising a near-total undoing of Orban’s hostility toward Kiev. Securing his support for something like the Carpathian Eight would have taken only minor concessions, namely some progress on the Transcarpathian issue.
Instead, Zelensky treated Hungary’s participation in the initiative as a given, and Sybiga reacted with petulant indignation when he was told ‘no’. Beyond the Carpathian region, with supplies of money and weapons running low, ‘no’ is a word that they might soon get used to hearing.

articles.title: EU removes two Russian billionaires from sanctions list
articles.body:
BRUSSELS — Two of Russia’s wealthiest men could soon be free to operate inside the EU after the bloc moved to lift restrictions on them and their empires as part of a high-stakes diplomatic play.
Capitals struck a deal on Tuesday to cut Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the sanctions list, five diplomats told POLITICO, granted anonymity to speak frankly.
For more than a week, France had been holding up the EU’s entire framework of individual sanctions in an unexpected standoff, risking the expiry of the 3,000-odd listings if they weren’t renewed. Earlier talks ended without a deal Monday night after Baltic nations initially refused to sign off.
Advertisement
Paris launched a surprise campaign earlier this month calling for sanctions to be dropped on mining and telecoms billionaire Usmanov and citing a “national security” issue at play. Luxembourg, meanwhile, had long been asking for the delisting of banking magnate Fridman, who is suing the country for access to assets frozen by the Grand Duchy.
A number of countries — including Nordic and Baltic nations — had warned the move could jeopardize the entire sanctions list, leading others to lobby for their own narrow interests. The breakthrough came after Latvia, which had been the most vocal opponent, agreed to abstain on the plan.
As part of the deal, the current selection of names will be frozen for three years, effectively sidelining further debate until 2029. The agreement was due to take effect if capitals submitted their written consent by 6 p.m. on Tuesday.
“It is done,” said one of the diplomats. “The question is what Baltic countries got in return.”
Latvia defends deal
Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs defended Riga’s climb-down, saying Latvia would “continue to advocate for the imposition of additional EU sanctions on Russia.” In a statement on the Latvian government website, the PM also noted that his had been “the only EU member state” to oppose the removal of “politically motivated individuals” from the individual sanctions list “until the very end.”
At the same time, he revealed, French President Emmanuel Macron had agreed to start talks with Latvia on its accession to France’s nuclear deterrence initiative, and “also expressed his commitment to strengthening France’s military presence in Latvia, especially in the field of air defense.”
“Such a commitment will strengthen not only the security of Latvia but also of the entire NATO eastern flank,” he added.
Advertisement
EU capitals have struck a deal to remove Russia’s Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the sanctions list.@benjaminhaddad called the outcome a win for European solidarity.
France had riled other EU members by announcing its support for Usmanov at short notice, saying only that it was related to “a specific national security issue” and that Paris “wishes to respond positively to international partners who have approached us regarding Mr. Usmanov.”
Still, its European Affairs Minister Benjamin Haddad called Tuesday’s outcome a win for European solidarity.
“We keep a very strong united front on the sanctions on Russia,” Haddad told POLITICO. “We have these discussions. You have consideration of national security and others among member states. But the most important is that we’ve shown once again our unity and our resolve to put economic pressure on Russia for its war of aggression.”
Ukraine slams 'shameful' arrangement
Kyiv led criticism of the sanctions list maneuver, with Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha describing the delisting of Usmanov and Fridman as “shameful and unjustifiable.”
“Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans,” he wrote on X.
The Financial Times reported that the delisting was part of a deal that could see French nationals released from detention in Azerbaijan. Paris has significantly stepped up its role in the South Caucasus in support of Armenia, a pro-EU democracy that has spent decades locked in conflict with Azerbaijan.
Advertisement
But some were concerned about the precedent that could set. “If the reports are confirmed, Europe must not turn sanctions into a bargaining chip,” said Latvian MEP Rihards Kols, a member of the Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee. “France has every right and duty to seek the release of its citizens. But the price cannot be relief for a Russian oligarch sanctioned for his links to the Putin regime.”
Ukraine’s Sybiha noted that member countries could still individually push back against the transaction. “There is still a way to spoil the celebrations in Moscow, he wrote. “I urge all EU member states to announce now that they will impose their own national sanctions on these two individuals [Usmanov and Fridman].”
The Latvian PM promised Latvia would do just that, and would “continue to use all legal instruments at its disposal to prevent the release of these persons’ funds and economic resources in Latvia.”
Info impasse
A handful of countries privately expressed frustration that further information had not been provided at Coreper, the meeting of ambassadors where sanctions rollover decisions are taken.
“Ambassadors were told that there are national security reasons. Coreper is not the right place to discuss those in detail,” said a senior French diplomat who was granted anonymity to speak frankly about the sensitive discussions last week. “Member states were told a week ago that if they needed more precision, they could get it through the appropriate channels.”
Usmanov has consistently denied supporting Russia’s war effort, rejected the idea he is an oligarch, and campaigned for his removal from the sanctions list. Fridman has likewise argued the seizure of his assets is unlawful.

articles.title: Retreat; The only option facing US to exit from Iran war?
articles.body:
The war of aggression waged by the US, after months of conflict, has yet to achieve Washington’s maximalist objectives while simultaneously driving up military and economic costs for the United States.
In this regard, Colonel Daniel Davis—a retired US Army officer and military analyst—believes that if Donald Trump wishes to emerge from a war with Iran with what could be termed a "victory," he must achieve objectives far beyond merely delivering military blows; these objectives include fundamentally altering Iran's political and military structures and eliminating the country's capacity to continue its missile and drone operations. From Davis's perspective, the fundamental problem is that the US military lacks the capacity to impose such an outcome.
This remark cannot be viewed merely as a personal stance; the issue Davis raises touches upon one of the fundamental challenges of warfare for Washington: the distinction between "military superiority" and "political victory." While the United States could leverage its air, naval, and intelligence capabilities to strike key targets in Iran and inflict significant damage on military infrastructure, turning this military superiority into a lasting shift in a nation's behavior or political structure is an entirely different matter.
The official and media reports also indicate that the war has not been without cost for the United States. According to estimates by the US Congressional Budget Office, the country's military operations had cost approximately $38 billion by August 1, a figure that rises by an average of about $3 billion per month. A report by the US Department of War Inspector General has also highlighted ammunition shortages and bottlenecks in production and replenishment capacities.
On the other hand, an assessment by the US Congressional Research Service indicates that by September 2026, the conflict has effectively reached a state of mutual attrition; this means that despite the damage it has sustained, Iran retains the capability to continue its attacks, while the United States and its partners face constraints regarding military capacity, economic costs, and political pressures. The report outlines four primary paths for Washington: maintaining the status quo, securing a ceasefire, escalating military operations, or negotiating a broader agreement.
This situation clears a significant part of Davis’s argument. If the US objective is merely to degrade a portion of Iran’s military capabilities, Washington can point to its operational achievements. However, if the goal is to completely eliminate Iran’s capacity for a military response, alter its political structure, and establish a new order, the gap between what is militarily feasible and what is politically achievable widens considerably.
A more significant issue is that the continuation of the war would not necessarily narrow this gap. While an escalation of attacks could inflict greater damage on Iran, it would simultaneously drive up costs for the United States and heighten the risk of the conflict spreading across the region. In recent weeks, Washington has remained undecided regarding the continuation or resumption of military operations. On September 17, Trump spoke of approaching a critical decision point concerning the war, stating that he was weighing various options for the future course of operations.
Amidst this situation, the discussion regarding US military capabilities has also gained greater significance. Recent reports indicate a depletion of certain ammunition stockpiles and strain on US production capacity—an issue that extends beyond a potential conflict with Iran and could impact Washington’s readiness for other contingencies, particularly those involving major powers.
From this perspective, the "withdrawal" Davis speaks of does not merely signify the physical departure of U.S. forces from the region. The core issue is devising a political exit strategy from the war—one that allows Washington to halt military operations without explicitly admitting defeat and to define the war's outcome through an agreement or new regional arrangements.
This is precisely the point where the conflict with Iran has become a strategic dilemma for the Trump administration. While prolonging the conflict might exert greater pressure on Iran, it offers no guarantee that America’s maximalist objectives will be achieved. Conversely, backing down or accepting a ceasefire could be interpreted within the US political landscape as a departure from the initially stated goals.
Consequently, Washington’s primary challenge is no longer merely whether the U.S. has the capacity to deliver further blows; the more critical question is whether those blows can yield the political outcome the U.S. desires. Daniel Davis’s position focuses precisely on this disconnect: a nation may possess air and military superiority on the battlefield yet fail to translate that advantage into its intended political result.
From this perspective, if Washington concludes that maximalist war objectives cannot be achieved through military means, a retreat might not signify an end to the pressure on Iran, but rather a shift in the tools of pressure—moving from direct warfare to negotiations, sanctions, and regional containment. Ultimately, the factor determining how the war concludes will not be merely the extent of U.S. capacity to sustain attacks, but the balance between the cost of continuing the war and the achievable political gains.
MNA

articles.title: The Pentagon has unveiled its secret weapon: two idiotic influencers | Arwa Mahdawi
articles.body:
We’re now approaching month seven of a war against Iran that Donald Trump repeatedly assured us would be over in a matter of weeks. Prices are rising, troop morale is plummeting, and there is little evidence things will improve.
The situation is so desperate that the decision makers at the Pentagon have decided to bring out the big guns. I’m not talking about nuclear weapons, although Trump recently threatened to “blow the entire nation [of Iran] up”. No, I’m talking about influencers Jake and Logan Paul, who are famous for doing idiotic stunts on YouTube and getting hit in the face during boxing matches. Last Thursday, Pete Hegseth’s Department of Defense or whatever they’re calling it these days (the Department of War Crimes?) welcomed the Paul brothers to Washington DC “to meet with our warriors” and deliver a motivational speech. In response, former Republican congressman and air force officer Adam Kinzinger wrote, “We aren’t a serious country at the moment.” That about sums it up.
The Paul brothers, to be fair, rose to the occasion as best they could. In a speech which channelled Churchill, if Churchill had suffered several major blows to the head, Logan said that touring the Pentagon had been “a cool experience”. Albeit not quite as cool as being deployed to fight and possibly die in an illegal bombing campaign started by president Trump, a convicted felon, on the advice of Benjamin Netanyahu, an accused war criminal. “I don’t think there is any greater commitment to sacrifice than those who are willing to live, die and fight for their country,” Logan said. Which is why you won’t see him doing it; easier to pocket millions fighting on TV.
As well as giving a pep talk to the military, Jake met up with treasury secretary Scott Bessent and the US treasurer to discuss how “to get more young Americans financially empowered.” That must have been an interesting chat considering how, back in 2023, the Securities and Exchange Commission charged the YouTuber with unlawfully promoting crypto assets without disclosing that he was being paid to do so; he eventually settled without admitting or denying the charges. (Logan has also faced a lawsuit linked to a dodgy crypto venture, although the case was eventually dismissed). Exactly the sort of person you want the treasury secretary expending energy talking to when US debt recently topped $40tn for the first time ever and a financial crisis seems to be around the corner.
Just how Jake Paul and Bessent hope to financially empower young Americans is unclear. But it is unlikely to be via the traditional method of working hard at school and then going to university. Jake very much shares the Trump administration’s contempt for education. In 2020 he tweeted that he’s “sick of our education system and how it’s teaching kids 0 real life skills for them to secure there [sic.] own future.” He also once described high school as “kids sitting in Geography to learn where Timbuktu is for no reason.” The reason you learn where Timbuktu is, Jake, is so the US can overthrow it after they’re done with Iran and Greenland.
There has always been a strong vein of anti-intellectualism in US politics. “[T]he subordination of men of ideas to men of emotional power or manipulative skill are hardly innovations of the twentieth century,” Richard Hofstadter wrote in his 1963 book Anti-intellectualism in American Life. “[T]hey are inheritances from American Protestantism.” But while this may not be a new impulse, the Trump administration’s embrace of ignorance is doing damage that can’t be easily undone. The US is stuck in a vicious vacuousness cycle: the Trump administration has slashed research funding and disrupted thousands of grants, leading many promising young academics to flee the US. As expertise is eliminated and critical thinking purged from government institutes, chancers like the Paul brothers are elevated.
Still, I suppose we should count our blessings, before even they are affected by Iran-induced inflation. At least the boneheaded Paul brothers are simply having meetings with high-level Trump administration officials. At least they’re not directly involved with military or economic policy. Although, the way things are going it’s only a matter of time. “I’m going to make a prediction that you will be, in the not-too-distant future, running for political office,” Trump told Jake, who has been a vocal Maga supporter, on stage at a rally earlier this year. “You have my complete and total endorsement.” Could another blond buffoon with zero qualifications become president of the US? Tune in to find out in the next season of America: the Empire Implodes

articles.title: Russia is holding Ukraine’s south with convicts: 69 percent have records. And they’re fighting where civilians live
articles.body:
More than two-thirds of the Russian soldiers holding the Zaporizhzhia front carry criminal records. Ukraine's "South" grouping says a third of them enlisted to escape prosecution, most are over 30, and no fresh reinforcements are arriving, spokesperson Anastasia Shevchenko told Ukrinform.
The reasons they signed up track with that: 31 percent enlisted to dodge criminal liability, 24 percent for money, 26 percent on ordinary contracts, and 13 percent through mobilization. It is Russia's prison pipeline in a single snapshot, a model that has pulled well over 100,000 inmates into the war with pardons and suspended sentences and thrown many of them at Ukrainian lines in disposable assault waves.
"It is worth noting that 69 percent of the Russian personnel have a criminal record," Shevchenko said.
The model dates to Wagner's prison recruiting in 2022 and has run under the Defense Ministry since.
A middle-aged force holds the line
The men are not young. More than a third, 36 percent, are between 31 and 40; another 24 percent are 41 to 50; 31 percent are 21 to 30; and just 9 percent are 20 or under.
This is a force of grown men with records, not fresh conscripts, and it points to who Russia can still find willing to fight in the south: people with little to lose and a sentence to escape among Ukrainian civilians, women and children.
The prison pipeline runs dry
What Shevchenko did not report is any sign of that force being rebuilt. Russia has enough men and equipment to keep fighting on the Zaporizhzhia front, she says, but no substantial replenishment is coming.
That fits a wider problem for Russia: its supply of convict recruits is thinning as word of the front's lethality spreads through the prisons, with some inmates now signing military contracts only to bolt on the way to the front, in one case killing their escort to get away.
Russia's practice of replenishing its ranks from prisons is breaking down, and officials are resorting to ever more coercive measures to keep the flow going.

articles.title: Ukraine and France Sign Contract for Air Defense Radars and Interceptor Missiles
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine and France Sign Contract for Air Defense Radars and Interceptor Missiles
Ukraine and France have signed a contract for the supply of air defense radars and interceptor missiles, French President Emmanuel Macron announced on September 22.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“We are strengthening its [Ukraine’s] air defense by signing a contract for the supply of radars, as well as the supply of interceptors,” Macron wrote on X.
The French president did not specify the types or number of radars and interceptor missiles covered by the agreement, nor did he provide a timeline for their delivery.
The agreement was announced following talks between Macron and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, which focused primarily on security and a winter support package for Ukraine.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine is also prepared to secure additional SAMP/T air defense systems and missiles using financial resources available under an EU loan.
The two countries are also working toward potentially producing SAMP/T systems and their missiles in Ukraine, according to Zelenskyy.
In parallel, Ukraine and its partners are advancing the joint FREYJA anti-ballistic missile program, with Zelenskyy saying Kyiv expects the first results as early as this year.
“We are doing everything we can to strengthen the protection of our people,” Zelenskyy said.
The air defense cooperation comes as France and Ukraine also deepen ties in combat aviation. France is preparing to begin initial training for Ukrainian pilots expected to transition to Rafale fighter jets as Kyiv moves toward integrating the French-made aircraft into its fleet.

articles.title: Jet-powered Russian drones strain Ukraine's air defences
articles.body:
Jet-powered Russian drones strain Ukraine's air defences
KYIV, Sept 22 - Vasyl, a portable rocket operator in one of Ukraine's many mobile air defence groups, was dismayed when he checked his screen. The Russian jet-powered Shahed drone moving towards his position was flying far too high for him to shoot it down.
"Before, Shaheds used to fly lower — one or 1.5 kilometres (above ground) and we could work on them," said Vasyl, who goes by the call sign Racoon, while on a mission to protect the capital Kyiv and the surrounding region with a shoulder-fired ground-to-air missile.
"But jet-powered drones now fly at four, five, even seven kilometres. It's not realistic for us to down them," the 26-year-old said.
Since Russia started widely using jet-powered drones this summer, hundreds have crashed into Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities in recent weeks, evading air defences. The new drones fly at high speeds and high altitudes, blurring the line between drones and cruise missiles.
The result has been disruption to businesses, government and ordinary life on a much bigger scale than in the previous four-and-a-half years of the war since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
In the first three weeks of September, Russia launched 2,100 jet-powered attack drones and 136 missiles at Ukraine, killing 288 people, including four children, according to Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi.
In August, Russia launched more than 2,800 such drones, he said. Moscow denies targeting civilians despite the growing civilian death toll and the devastation caused to cities across Ukraine.
HIGH ALTITUDES AND SECONDS TO REACT
Vasyl and his mobile drone-hunting crew of three people have only seconds to react to attacks by jet-powered drones, instead of minutes with the propeller versions of the Shahed. Russia is also now launching drones round the clock instead of largely at night.
"It's aiming to wear down our air defences," said Vasyl, adding that drones had been flying all day. "It all takes its toll, because we're out on duty and we're not really getting any sleep."
Ukraine is intercepting only about 60% of the jet-powered drones, compared to the more than 90% of earlier models that were routinely intercepted, said Yurii Ihnat, the Ukrainian air force's spokesperson.
The new drones are more expensive than propeller versions, but are still cheaper than the cruise missiles that Russia has been firing at Ukraine.
BROADER RANGE OF TARGETS
In recent months, Moscow has systematically targeted the pillars of Ukraine's economy including its Black Sea grain ports, railways and the steel and logistics sectors.
Hundreds of thousands of square meters of warehouses and commercial properties have been destroyed in Ukraine. Russia has disrupted supplies of food products, medicines, and other daily-use products for the first time since the early days of the war.
Moscow has used the new tactic as its advances on the battlefield stalled. Ukraine has also ramped up its own strikes on Russia, hitting its oil and fuel infrastructure and weapon production companies.
The shift in Russian tactics was anticipated, said Fedir Venislavskyi, a lawmaker in President Volodymyr Zelenskiy's ruling party and a member of parliament's security committee, adding that efforts were now underway to come up with effective defences.
Ukrainian officials have reported several successful combat uses of drone interceptors against jet-propelled Russian drones, but their mass production and other potential solutions would require time and money.
Money is in short supply: Zelenskiy has announced an unexpected defence funding shortfall for this year of $27 billion as the war has become more expensive. Kyiv is in talks with its partners on how to cover the gap.
"I believe that we will resolve the issue of jet-powered drones in the short term. But as with all other aspects of buying weapons, everything comes down to financial resources," Venislavskyi said. REUTERS

articles.title: UK deploys RAF tanker to refuel Saudi jets amid Houthi attacks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UK deploys RAF tanker to refuel Saudi jets amid Houthi attacks
Britain will deploy an RAF tanker to refuel Saudi warplanes amid renewed Houthi attacks on the kingdom, as an escalating battle for strategic territory in Yemen threatens to further destabilise the Red Sea region.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he approved a Saudi request for "defensive air-to-air refuelling", with a single RAF Voyager expected to begin operating from Britain's RAF Akrotiri base in Cyprus in the coming days.
The deployment is expected to last several weeks initially, although Burnham said it would be kept under review.
British officials said the mission would be limited to refuelling Saudi aircraft involved in defending the kingdom against Houthi missile and drone attacks, rather than supporting Saudi strikes inside Yemen.
The move nevertheless expands Britain's military involvement alongside Saudi Arabia at a time when fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed forces has intensified dramatically.
Earlier this year, the UK deployed its Sky Sabre air defence system to Saudi Arabia to help protect the kingdom against Iranian missile attacks.
Burnham linked the latest deployment to regional stability and Britain's economic interests, saying disruption to major energy routes needed to be prevented as turmoil across the region puts pressure on global energy supplies.
The British deployment comes after the Houthis made sweeping gains along Yemen's Red Sea coast, including the capture of the strategic port city of Mocha and territory around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
Battle for strategic heights
Fighting has since shifted towards the Kahboub Mountains, a range of strategic heights spanning parts of Taiz and Lahj provinces and separating the Red Sea coast from areas of southern Yemen held by forces aligned with the internationally recognised government.
Five Yemeni military sources told Reuters that the Houthis were attempting to seize the heights in an effort to cut off remaining Saudi-backed positions along the Red Sea coast from government-held territory further south.
Control of the mountains could allow the Houthis to consolidate their rapid coastal advances by dominating routes connecting the Red Sea coast with southern Yemen.
Government-aligned forces have meanwhile mounted a counteroffensive aimed at preventing the Houthis from securing the high ground and preserving their ability to push back towards the coast.
The renewed fighting has drawn Saudi Arabia more directly back into the conflict, with Riyadh carrying out air strikes in Yemen while facing repeated Houthi missile and drone attacks on its own territory.
Saudi Arabia has simultaneously sought international assistance to contain the Houthi advance.
US President Donald Trump considered ordering American strikes against the group over the weekend following repeated appeals from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, but ultimately decided to hold off, according to US media reports.
Saudi Arabia has also turned to China, asking Beijing to use its influence with Iran to restrain the Houthis.
China subsequently privately asked Tehran to help rein in the group, Reuters reported last week, citing three Iranian sources familiar with the discussions.
Riyadh's appeals came after the Houthi advance along the Red Sea coast and around Bab al-Mandab heightened concerns over Saudi oil exports and international shipping.
The escalation comes as traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the principal route for Gulf oil exports, has already been severely disrupted by the wider conflict involving Iran and the United States.
That has increased the strategic importance of the Red Sea route through Bab al-Mandab, with Burnham saying Britain needed to help keep vital energy routes open.

articles.title: Russian forces attack Dnipro, Kryvyi Rih and Pavlohrad with ballistic missiles
articles.body:
Russian forces attack Dnipro, Kryvyi Rih and Pavlohrad with ballistic missiles
Russian forces launched ballistic missile strikes on Dnipropetrovsk Oblast on the night of 21-22 September, with explosions reported in the cities of Dnipro, Kryvyi Rih and Pavlohrad.
Source: Oleksandr Vilkul, Head of Kryvyi Rih Defence Council; Ukraine's Air Force, Oleksandr Hanzha, Head of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Military Administration; monitoring Telegram channels
Details: Hanzha said that Russian forces had simultaneously struck industrial facilities in three cities in the oblast. Fires broke out at sites in Dnipro, Kryvyi Rih and Pavlohrad.
Vilkul confirmed the missile strike on Kryvyi Rih.
"The city is under attack from ballistic missiles. There may be more strikes," he said.
He added that the Russians were also launching cruise missiles towards the same targets.
Early reports from monitoring channels and the military indicate that four ballistic missiles struck Dnipro and four hit Kryvyi Rih, while at least three more missiles attacked Pavlohrad.
Background:
- At 01:58, the Air Force warned of the threat of Russian ballistic weapons being launched from Russia's Voronezh.
- Shortly afterwards, the military detected high-speed targets moving towards Dnipropetrovsk Oblast.
