articles.title: Fake passport images claim Zelenskyy and family chose Israel as homeland
articles.body:
A photo amassing thousands of views on social media allegedly shows a scan of Zelenskyy's passport, with Israel as his homeland. Not only are the allegations false, but they've been doing the rounds since 2023.
A fake photo circulating online of two alleged Israeli passports belonging to Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his wife, Olena Zelenska, allegedly shows that the Ukrainian president and his family have chosen Israel as their homeland instead of Ukraine.
The Facebook post was published at the beginning of September alongside the caption: "You can twist it any way you like, but we always come back to the same point: Zelenskyy and his family have a homeland of choice that inspires, protects and supports him in everything he does, and that homeland is certainly not Ukraine. This is common knowledge, just as it is common knowledge who his backers are at the top of the Ukrainian establishment, but people prefer to turn a blind eye so as not to disturb those pulling the strings. Shalom."
There is no truth behind these claims. The Cube, Euronews' fact-checking team, contacted Ukrainian official sources who denied them.
Furthermore, Ukrainian public officials are not permitted to hold multiple citizenships, unlike members of the general public, under a recent law which officially came into effect in January of this year.
Additionally, the false passport belonging to Zelenska lists the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic as her place of birth. This is inaccurate, as official identity documents issued for individuals born in Ukraine before independence routinely list Ukraine rather than the defunct Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic, which was one of the constituent republics of the Soviet Union from 1922 until 1991.
The Cube, Euronews' fact-checking team, also ran it through the image detector Hive Moderation, which revealed it to be AI-generated.
The fake passport appears to have been created based on a sample template published on the Council of Europe website.
Fake Zelenskyy passports resurfaced
It's not the first time false passports attributed to Zelenskyy and Zelenska have circulated online.
In April 2026, an image of an alleged Israeli passport of Zelenskyy was shared on Instagram, X and Facebook, gathering thousands of views, likes and reshares.
These posts claimed that the Ukrainian president was an agent for Israel's intelligence agency, whose main mission was "to Ukrainianise Europe and lead it to its own self-destruction".
In addition to a significant portion of the passport being cropped in the image, there is a spelling error in Zelenskyy's name.
According to the president's official website, his last name is stylised as "Zelenskyy" in English, not "Zelensky", as the alleged passport shows.
In fact, stories about Zelenskyy and Zelenska's alleged passport have been doing the rounds since at least 2023.
For instance, a photo of the first lady was shared on pro-Russian channels and in several Facebook posts.
In one of these posts, the caption can read: "While Ukrainian President Zelensky travels the world begging for money and weapons for his war, his wife spent a lovely vacation in Israel and even obtained an Israeli passport. Interestingly, is Mrs Zelensky preparing for a possible escape from Ukraine?"
All of these posts follow the same playbook: use an AI-generated passport to invent a scandal with some real elements to target Ukraine and undermine support from its allies, as Russia's war against the country continues.
These techniques are common tactics used among pro-Russian networks in their disinformation campaigns.
The posts about the alleged Israeli passports stand at odds with one of Russian President Vladimir Putin's supposed justifications for his full-scale invasion: when it began in February 2022, Putin pledged to oversee the "demilitarisation and de-Nazification" of Ukraine.
However, as the grandson of a Holocaust survivor, Zelenskyy has Jewish origins and has previously addressed the series of attacks on his religious background by the Kremlin.
"How can I be a Nazi?" Zelenskyy said in 2022, just before the full-scale invasion, in a video address directed at the Russian people in the Russian language. "Explain it to my grandfather, who went through the entire war in the infantry of the Soviet army, and died a colonel in an independent Ukraine."

articles.title: Ukraine attacks radiation monitor at Europe’s largest nuclear power plant
articles.body:
Ukraine attacks radiation monitor at Europe’s largest nuclear power plant
A Ukrainian drone strike has damaged a radiation monitoring post near the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant, the facility said on Tuesday.
The station was located near the village of Ivanovka, around 13 km from the nuclear plant, and formed part of the system used to track radiation levels in the surrounding area. Such posts regularly collect data on background radiation, allowing specialists to detect changes and respond quickly if conditions deteriorate.
The plant said the remaining monitoring equipment and capacity were sufficient to continue observing radiation levels, but noted that the loss of the station has reduced the amount of data that could be quickly gathered from that particular area.
In the event of an emergency, the loss could become significant as specialists would need reliable readings from multiple locations to determine the nature and scale of any changes in radiation levels.
At the same time, the facility stressed that losing one post did not mean radiation monitoring had stopped and did not itself indicate any radiation threat.
Nevertheless, it warned that further attacks on radiation monitoring infrastructure could reduce specialists’ ability to obtain information quickly and comprehensively in the event of an emergency.
Tuesday’s strike follows a series of attacks on and around the ZNPP that Moscow has blamed on Ukraine. Earlier this month, the Russian nuclear corporation Rosatom said Ukrainian strikes hit tankers delivering emergency diesel fuel to the plant, killing two Russian servicemen and wounding several others. The fuel is used to power the backup generators needed for critical safety systems if the facility loses its external electricity supply.
In July, a drone strike on a service vehicle near the plant’s industrial site also killed ZNPP chief engineer Aleksandr Yakovlev and his driver. Rosatom has accused Ukrainian forces of using drones to scatter anti-personnel mines on roads used by plant employees and residents of nearby Energodar.
Russia has repeatedly warned that continued attacks around the facility risk triggering a nuclear emergency with consequences extending beyond the immediate area.
Moscow has also criticized the International Atomic Energy Agency, which maintains a presence at the plant, for reporting explosions, drones and other military activity around the ZNPP without publicly identifying Ukraine as responsible.

articles.title: What will UK's Ed Miliband focus on at his first UNGA?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
What will UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband focus on at his first UNGA?
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is attending his first United Nations General Assembly high-level week since taking office, arriving in New York with the Middle East and Sudan among the major crises confronting world leaders.
In his first nine weeks as foreign secretary, Miliband has already taken a tougher stance on Israel's illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, announcing plans to ban imports from settlements and impose sanctions on individuals and companies involved in settlement activity.
But how will Britain's new foreign secretary approach these issues on the world stage? And where does he stand on other major questions facing this year's gathering, including the US-Israel war on Iran, Sudan's devastating civil war and nuclear disarmament?
Will Miliband discuss Israel and Palestine?
Israel and Palestine are expected to feature prominently in Miliband's diplomacy in New York.
Earlier this month, the UK announced plans to prohibit imports of goods from illegal Israeli settlements and introduce sanctions against individuals and companies supporting, facilitating or benefiting from settlement activity.
The measures followed Miliband's condemnation of settlement expansion and settler violence in the occupied West Bank. He has also repeatedly backed a two-state solution and said Israeli settlements are a "flagrant breach of international law".
However, Miliband has rejected the wider Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement, drawing a distinction between measures targeting illegal settlements and a broader boycott of Israel.
Daniel Forti, the International Crisis Group's Head of UN Affairs, told The New Arab that Miliband "will be closely involved in discussions around Palestine and the Two State Solution, where UN-backed diplomacy has fallen by the wayside at the expense of the Board of Peace".
"States will watch closely to see how UK officials defend their sanctions on Israel for expanding settlements in the West Bank, and how fiery a response they receive from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu."
Netanyahu is also expected to attend this week's gathering in New York. He responded angrily to Britain's settlement measures, while the Israeli government has strongly rejected international pressure over its policies in the West Bank.
What about Sudan?
Sudan is also emerging as a significant part of Miliband's first UNGA agenda.
Britain is the UN Security Council penholder on Sudan and has pushed for stronger international action as the country's civil war and humanitarian crisis continue.
Speaking in New York on Monday, Miliband described Sudan as "the worst humanitarian crisis this century" and set out three priorities for international action: diplomacy aimed at securing a ceasefire and eventual civilian government, improved humanitarian access, and greater protection for civilians.
He also called for stronger scrutiny of countries and networks supplying weapons and other support that are fuelling the conflict.
Forti said Miliband would use his time in New York to raise the profile of the war.
"Miliband will also hope to use his time in New York [to] raise the profile of the on-going war in Sudan. The UK leads the Security Council's discussions on the country but has been unable to rally its members around a common strategy to back various diplomatic efforts," he said.
"The UK will likely use a range of side events during UNGA to remind world leaders of the war's horrific toll and the urgent need to bring the warring parties back to the negotiating table."
What has Miliband said about the war on Iran?
Miliband's response to the US-Israel-led war on Iran has combined calls for diplomacy with a focus on the conflict's economic impact on Britain.
Following talks with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Miliband said Britain would work towards a ceasefire, while repeatedly highlighting the consequences of instability in the Middle East and disruption to the Strait of Hormuz for energy prices and the cost of living in the UK.
He has also maintained Britain's longstanding position that Iran must not acquire a nuclear weapon.
In a foreign policy speech earlier this year, Miliband said the objective should be to move "from conflict to containment", using coordinated international action and diplomacy to prevent Iran from rebuilding capabilities that threaten regional states and international shipping.
Iran will also be represented at this week's meetings in New York, potentially making diplomacy surrounding the conflict another important issue on the sidelines of the General Assembly.
What is Miliband's stance on nuclear weapons?
Nuclear weapons will also be on the UN agenda this week, with a high-level meeting marking the International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons.
The meeting is intended to give UN member states an opportunity to reaffirm their commitment to nuclear disarmament.
Miliband has historically supported maintaining Britain's nuclear deterrent and voted in favour of replacing the UK's Trident nuclear weapons system while serving as an MP.
Since becoming foreign secretary, his comments on nuclear proliferation have focused primarily on Iran, repeatedly stressing that Tehran must not acquire a nuclear weapon.
It remains unclear whether Miliband will attend the UN nuclear disarmament meeting. His participation, or absence, could nevertheless draw attention to the tension between Britain's support for international nuclear non-proliferation and its continued maintenance of its own nuclear deterrent.

articles.title: Russia’s SVR comments on yet another EU’s attempt to seize sovereign Russian assets
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 22. /TASS/. European bureaucrats fear that without seizing Russian assets they will not be able to indefinitely fund the corrupt Kiev regime, Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) said in a press release on Tuesday.
According to the SVR, they are discussing proposals at the expert level to create a new supranational entity where Russian assets could be ‘hidden’ after being removed from the Euroclear depositary. Such a move would undermine the credibility of pan-European institutions, the SVR warned.
TASS has compiled key statements from the SVR.
Operation to steal Russian assets
European officials fear that without seizing Russian assets, they "will not be able to endlessly fund the corrupt Kiev regime, which constitutes the expenditure side of NATO’s conflict with Russia," the SVR argued.
EU leaders are rushing to carry out the operation to confiscate Russian assets before next year’s elections in a number of European countries: "EU leaders have a vital interest in completing the operation to steal Russian assets before the elections in a number of European countries in 2027."
EU’s plan to seize Russian assets
According to information made available to the SVR, minds in Brussels are "still all hyped up over plans to misappropriate the Bank of Russia’s assets frozen in the EU."
The EU is discussing proposals at the expert level to remove Russian assets from the Euroclear depositary: "This time around, they are discussing proposals at the expert level on creating a new supranational entity where Russian assets could be ‘hidden’ after being removed from the Euroclear depositary."
Potential impact for EU
The SVR warned the EU that attempts to confiscate sovereign Russian assets may erode global confidence in pan-European institutions: "The current ruling elite in the EU should come to understand that its attempts to steal sovereign Russian assets will undermine the credibility of pan-European institutions." "Countries in the Global South will no longer consider European jurisdictions as a safe haven," the SVR said. "For Europe will not be able to maintain the stability of its own financial system without relying on large foreign holders of European securities, such as China, India, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Singapore. So, the thief will be punished in any case," the SVR argued.
EU’s attempts to remove Russian assets from Euroclear depositary
On September 2, Euractiv reported that the EU is considering an option to remove the frozen Russian assets from the Belgian jurisdiction and transfer them away from the Brussels-based clearing house Euroclear into a "completely new legal vehicle."
According to the website, the proposal was presented to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen as a creative effort to override Belgian resistance to using the funds held at Euroclear.
On August 29, Belgium blocked the latest attempt by four EU member states to revive discussions on the possible expropriation of frozen Russian assets, Belgian Defense and Foreign Trade Minister Theo Francken told VRT television.
The kingdom declared the plan to expropriate and use €200 billion in sovereign Russian assets immobilized at Euroclear in Belgium to support Ukraine’s military operations "non-negotiatible," he said.
Belgium blocked the European Commission’s initial attempt to appropriate the funds in December 2025.
Russian assets freeze
The EU and the Group of Seven (G7) nations have frozen approximately €300 billion in Russian assets, with about €185 billion held at the Belgian depository Euroclear.
The EU is looking for ways to utilize these funds for Ukraine’s needs. It acknowledges a lack of legal mechanisms for such operations, which threaten to erode international investor confidence.
In December 2025, the Bank of Russia filed an 18.2-trillion-ruble ($216 bln) lawsuit against Euroclear with the Moscow Arbitration Court, seeking the return of frozen funds, the value of blocked securities, and lost profits. On May 15, the court ruled in favor of the Russian regulator.
By May 29, court bailiffs initiated almost 60 enforcement proceedings against Euroclear Bank to recover nearly 28 billion rubles ($332 mln), according to court and other materials seen by TASS.

articles.title: Houthis push for control of Yemen highlands as Trump is said to have called off strikes
articles.body:
Houthi fighters pushed to seize strategic heights in Yemen on Monday to cut off the Red Sea coast from remaining areas held by Saudi-backed forces, after a report that US President Donald Trump had called off American strikes on the group at the last minute.
A lightning advance by the Iran-backed group this month has extended the wider Middle East conflict to a new theater and further threatened global energy supplies. The US has so far rebuffed repeated pleas from Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to join the fight in Yemen.
The New York Times reported that the Trump administration had prepared to launch airstrikes on Sunday against the Houthis after fresh pleas from the Saudi crown prince. But the newspaper said Trump called off the airstrikes at the last minute, even as troops were loading bombs onto aircraft.
Reuters could not verify the Times' report. The US military's Central Command referred questions to the White House. The White House did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment.
Rashid al-Alimi, the Riyadh-based president of Yemen's Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government, asked Trump by phone on Sunday for US military help, four sources told Reuters. Two of the people, one Yemeni and one Western, said Trump made no direct pledge of support during the call.
Riyadh was apparently struck on Saturday for the first time since the escalation began, with explosions heard and smoke visible near the airport. The Houthis said they had fired missiles at the Saudi capital; the Saudis have not commented.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday he had agreed to Saudi Arabia's request to provide defensive air-to-air refueling for a limited time, a move he described as helping to stabilize the wider region. Britain and Saudi Arabia have been close military allies for decades, with Britain serving as one of the kingdom's largest arms suppliers.
A French diplomatic source said Paris was ready to help secure Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure in Yanbu on the Red Sea coast and the East-West pipeline corridor.
Where have the Houthis advanced to?
The Houthis, who have controlled Yemen's capital since 2014, seized the country's Red Sea coast this month in an advance that routed forces of the Saudi-backed government.
Saudi Arabia has launched hundreds of strikes in recent days on the fighters' positions in the highlands, the Houthis say.
According to the United Nations, nearly 700 people have been killed and thousands injured in the fighting. Nearly 130,000 Yemenis have fled their homes within Yemen, and more than 3,000 have fled by boat across the Red Sea to Africa.
Five Yemeni military sources told Reuters the Houthis were now seeking to seize strategic heights, known as the Kahboub Mountains, in two provinces, Taiz and Lahij, which separate the Red Sea coast from the government-held south.
Fighting has centered on the outskirts of the remote mountain Al-Wazi'iyah district in Taiz province, and Ras al-Ara along the Indian Ocean coast between the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the Red Sea's mouth and the government's base in Aden, the sources said.
"The government forces appear to remain largely in a defensive posture following the loss of the Bab el-Mandeb area, while the Houthis are seeking to maintain the momentum of their advance, despite being exposed to intensive air strikes," said Mohammed Al-Qadhi, a veteran Yemeni journalist now working as a political analyst.
"These mountains could become critical to determining whether the Houthis succeed in consolidating their recent territorial gains or whether government forces will be able to retain the positions necessary to mount a counteroffensive."
Will Trump strike the Houthis?
The surge in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis creates a dilemma for Trump, under pressure to help Saudi allies but anxious not to further expand the deeply unpopular war he launched alongside Israel as "Operation Epic Fury" in February against Iran.
The US bombed the Houthis for two months in early 2025, but Trump called off those strikes after reaching a ceasefire, and has kept out of the Yemen conflict since.
The Houthis' Red Sea advance risks cutting off the main alternative route Saudi Arabia has used for oil exports that bypass disruption through the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia has responded by increasing shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, where a small number of tankers are increasingly shuttling back and forth to bring out oil, charging record fees of as much as a quarter of the cargo's value to brave the wartime risk. They then transfer the oil to other ships in the Indian Ocean, bound for customers in Asia or elsewhere.
Traders say Saudi Arabia has sold 60 million barrels of oil both this month and next, to be loaded from off Oman on the far side of Hormuz. Satellite data shows Saudi exports through Hormuz reaching 2.9 million barrels per day in recent days, up from just 700,000 in August.
That has helped cap the global price of crude, which has retreated closer to $100 a barrel after approaching $110 last week. But consumers and industries are still paying record prices for some refined fuels, with the US retail price of diesel hitting another all-time high on Monday.
In the latest reported attack in Hormuz, Britain's UKMTO maritime security agency said a ship sailing into the strait had been hit with a projectile, causing minor injuries to crew. It also said it had learned of an earlier strike on a gas tanker.
Diplomacy in the wider conflict has largely been stalled since a June interim ceasefire agreement between the US and Iran collapsed within weeks. Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian is due to fly to New York on Tuesday to attend the UN General Assembly.

articles.title: Egypt shifts wheat purchases away from Russia and Ukraine as Black Sea trade costs rise
articles.body:
Egypt is increasing wheat purchases from France as it diversifies away from Russia and Ukraine, Reuters reported on 20 September, citing remarks made that Sunday by the country's Supply Minister Sherif Farouk, as quoted by television host Ahmed Moussa and confirmed afterwards by a ministry spokesperson.
Russian and Ukrainian strikes on each other's shipping are disrupting Black Sea trade routes used by both major wheat exporters, pushing up shipping costs and forcing grain buyers to navigate longer and more expensive alternatives. For Ukraine, a disrupted sea route means fewer or more expensive grain exports, putting pressure on farmers' incomes and the country's export earnings.
Egypt is one of the world's biggest wheat importers, and the grain feeds a subsidized bread program that tens of millions of Egyptians rely on. The supply minister also said Cairo had a 50,000-metric-ton wheat shipment en route from France, with further shipments from the country continuing, and that Egypt has stepped up its engagement with Bulgaria and Romania. Its wheat reserves cover more than six months of strategic consumption, he said.
War-risk costs climb as the high-risk zone widens
Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on each other's commercial shipping, and London's marine insurers widened the area they treat as high risk to the whole Black Sea. The Joint War Committee, which sets that listing for the Lloyd's market, extended its reporting requirements to the entire sea, and its guidance shapes what underwriters charge. War-risk premiums have surged as dozens of ships have been attacked in the Black Sea, and are adding hundreds of thousands of dollars to the cost of every seven-day voyage.
Russia was continuing attempts to destroy Ukraine's transport infrastructure and block its exports through the Black Sea, Ukrzaliznytsia said on 30 July. More than 90% of Ukraine's agricultural exports were shipped from ports in Odesa Oblast through a maritime corridor.
Ukraine's export capacity falls after July strikes
Following Russian strikes on Ukrainian ports on 10–12 July, the deepwater terminals' monthly handling capacity fell by about 2.5 million tons, from up to seven million to four or five, Barva Invest's Bohdan Kostetskyi said at the time. Industry sources told Reuters that four of 13 major terminals had stopped buying grain.
By mid-August, Ukrainian attacks and the suspension of navigation in the Sea of Azov since July had taken more than 90% of Russia's grain export capacity in the Azov–Black Sea basin offline, agricultural consultancy SovEcon said. Three Novorossiysk terminals were suspended, while the Taman terminal had halted operations in late July.
The Danube detour takes longer and costs more
Two vessels sailing from Izmail to Egypt took 26 days and an estimated 32 to 33 days, and a third bound for Izmir 28 to 29 days, against about 12 days for the Egypt run before the delays, Avalon Shipping operations manager Kateryna Kononenko told Ukrainian Shipping Magazine.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia facing Iranian proxies alone as US opts out of strikes - analysis
articles.body:
On September 11, an Iranian-backed militia in Iraq carried out an attack on Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline.
This came as the Houthis also advanced toward Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Saudi Arabia has now faced a potential two-front conflict over the last 10 days. Now Saudi Arabia has sent officials to the UN General Assembly (UNGA). Riyadh has also been wondering whether it will get military support from the US.
What is happening is that the US has advanced a sale of F-35s to Saudi Arabia. However, if the sale proceeds, the 5th-generation warplanes won’t arrive in Saudi Arabia for years. Riyadh needs to decide what to do now.
The Houthis have continued their threats over the last week. They have been fortifying the positions they captured near Bab el-Mandeb; they are pushing propaganda against Saudi Arabia and launching attacks on the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia. They have even threatened Mecca. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia’s allies, Pakistan and Turkey, do not appear to be stepping up.
Saudi Arabia is wary of going it alone. Arab News noted on Saturday that “Yemeni government forces clashed with Houthi fighters on several fronts in Marib on Saturday, advancing on Al-Mashjah front west of the city and forcing the Houthis to retreat, military sources said.” The sources added that the Armed Forces destroyed several Houthi vehicles during the fighting, according to an Al Arabiya report.
Saudi Arabia left alone in its time of need
Meanwhile, Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan arrived in New York on Saturday to lead the Kingdom’s delegation at the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, Arab News noted.
“The delegation includes Saudi Ambassador to the US Princess Reema bint Bandar, Minister of State for Foreign Affairs Adel Al-Jubeir, and King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Center Supervisor General Dr. Abdullah Al-Rabeeah, along with other officials.”
Saudi Arabia also said it had postponed its Red Sea International Film Festival to 2027. The New Arab media outlet noted that “Saudi Arabia has spent decades building its security partnership with Washington, buying billions of dollars in US weapons and cultivating close ties with successive American administrations.”
It said that “when Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman made a direct plea to US President Donald Trump for military help against Yemen’s Houthis, Washington ultimately stepped away. For two weeks, Trump had wrestled with whether to order US strikes on Houthi targets as the Iran-backed group intensified attacks on Saudi Arabia and made territorial gains in Yemen.”
The report, along with others, noted that the US has stepped back from strikes on the Houthis. This is important. Riyadh wants commitment. It has been fighting since 2015 in Yemen. Saudi Arabia has faced this dilemma before. In 2019, Iran attacked Saudi Arabia’s Abqaiq energy facility on the coast. This is similar to the September 11 attack on the East-West pipeline.
The message was clear both times. If Saudi Arabia responds, the attacks on strategic infrastructure will continue. Riyadh has more to lose than Iran or the Houthis or militias in Iraq. Saudi Arabia and US Central Command retaliated in July for militia attacks from Iraq. The attacks stopped for several weeks.
This big question for Riyadh at the UNGA is whether it can rally support and also work with Washington regarding the next steps in Yemen. The Houthis believe they are winning. Saudi Arabia will have to see how it can avoid a two-front conflict and also restore deterrence.

articles.title: Russia attacks 13 regions and Kyiv with drones and missiles overnight – Koretskyi
articles.body:
Russia attacks 13 regions and Kyiv with drones and missiles overnight – Koretskyi
Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said this in a Telegram post, according to Ukrinform.
"Another massive drone and missile attack on Ukrainian cities. The Russians are deliberately targeting businesses, farms, warehouses, railways, energy facilities and residential buildings. Thirteen regions and Kyiv came under attack overnight and this morning," the post reads.
According to the prime minister, four people were killed and six others injured in Dnipro as a result of a missile strike. A rescue operation is ongoing.
There was also serious damage in Kryvyi Rih and Pavlohrad.
In the Poltava, Vinnytsia and Zhytomyr regions, Russian forces targeted energy and railway infrastructure. Several power substations in different regions were also hit overnight.
In Kyiv, residential buildings were damaged and five people were injured as a result of the attack.
All necessary emergency services are currently working at the sites.
As reported, Ukraine's air defense forces neutralized one Kalibr cruise missile, eight Banderol missiles and 177 drones used by Russian forces to attack Ukraine from the evening of September 21.
Photo: Ukraine's State Emergency Service

articles.title: Russia Is Dropping More Glide Bombs on Ukraine Per Day Than US Did During Iran Air Campaign
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Is Dropping More Glide Bombs on Ukraine Per Day Than US Did During Iran Air Campaign
Russian forces dropped 8,766 guided aerial bombs on Ukraine in August 2026, bringing the daily rate of their use above that recorded for guided bomb strikes during the recent US air campaign against Iran.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Militarnyi on September 22, Russia used an average of 283 aerial bombs equipped with Universal Gliding and Correction Modules, known as UMPK, per day during August. The outlet based its comparison with US operations on Pentagon data and research by the Royal United Services Institute.
During the US-led Operation Epic Fury against Iran, American aircraft employed an estimated 211 to 237 guided aerial bombs per day, according to Militarnyi’s calculations.
The comparison concerns the rate at which guided aerial munitions were released rather than the overall scale, capabilities, targets, or operational conditions of the respective air campaigns.
Russia’s current rate remains below that recorded during the main phase of the US-led invasion of Iraq in 2003. Militarnyi estimated that US and coalition aircraft used roughly 509 precision-guided munitions per day during that period.
The 2003 Iraq campaign involved extensive use of precision-guided weapons. US Air Force data shows that 19,948 of the 29,199 munitions employed during the initial campaign were guided weapons.
Russia’s UMPK kits and the US-developed Joint Direct Attack Munition, or JDAM, are based on a broadly similar approach: adding guidance and control systems to existing stocks of conventional free-fall bombs rather than producing an entirely new weapon.
The US Air Force describes JDAM as a guidance kit that converts conventional unguided bombs into precision weapons using inertial navigation and GPS guidance.
Russia has pursued the same general concept with UMPK-equipped bombs, allowing aircraft to release modified conventional bombs from greater distances. RUSI reported in February 2025 that Russia had ordered more than 70,000 UMPK glide-bomb kits for that year alone as production expanded during the full-scale war.
The August figure illustrates the continuing expansion of Russia’s use of glide bombs against Ukraine. During the final ten days of July, Russian forces also struck Pavlohrad, around 75 kilometers from the front line, three times with guided aerial bombs, according to Militarnyi.
The outlet said the attacks could indicate renewed use of the jet-powered UMPB-5R extended-range bomb.
Russia has also expanded production of other relatively low-cost precision weapons. In September, The Wall Street Journal reported that Russia was rapidly moving new jet-powered systems, including the Geran-5 drone and Banderol cruise missile, from battlefield testing into serial production, with both weapons estimated to cost around $100,000 each.
Discuss this article:

articles.title: Russia, Ukraine escalate long-range strikes as civilian toll mounts: officials
articles.body:
Russia and Ukraine exchanged fresh long-range strikes on Tuesday, with Moscow saying it hit targets including a cargo vessel near the Black Sea port of Odessa and an oil refinery in Kremenchuk, while Russian officials reported a deadly Ukrainian drone attack in the Samara region.
Russia’s defence ministry said its forces struck a cargo ship delivering military equipment to Odessa and targeted the Kremenchuk refinery in central Ukraine. The claims could not be independently verified.
In Russia, Samara regional Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said Ukrainian drones struck civilian areas overnight, killing one person and injuring four. He said private homes and vehicles were among the sites hit.
The mayor of Samara, Ivan Noskov, said air defences had repelled a “massive” drone attack on the city, which lies more than 1,000 kilometres southeast of Moscow.
Deadly strikes reported in Dnipro
Russian attacks also killed at least two people in Dnipro, Ukrainian officials said, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was in New York for the United Nations General Assembly.
Dnipropetrovsk regional Governor Oleksandr Ganzha said missiles, drones and artillery struck four districts of the region.
In Dnipro, warehouses and a business were severely damaged, while six people were wounded.
Industrial facilities were also hit in Kryvyi Rih and Pavlohrad, according to Ukrainian authorities.
The latest attacks underscore the widening geographic reach of the Russia-Ukraine war’s long-range campaign, with both sides increasingly targeting industrial, energy, logistics and port infrastructure.
Recent strikes have also affected oil refineries and shipping facilities, adding pressure to already vulnerable supply networks.
Both Moscow and Kiev have repeatedly said their strikes are directed at military or strategic infrastructure, while officials on each side accuse the other of endangering civilians.

articles.title: At least 555 Ukrainians have faced treason and espionage charges from Russia during full-scale invasion, report says
articles.body:
Russia has accused at least 555 Ukrainian citizens of treason, espionage, and related crimes since the start of the full-scale war, accounting for nearly 38% of all known defendants in such cases. Of those, 266 had been listed in Ukraine’s official register of missing persons, according to a study by the human rights group Pervy Otdel (lit. “Department One”) and Parubets Analytics, which based their findings on court records, law enforcement statements, media reports, information from lawyers and relatives, and open-source investigations.
People are entered into Ukraine’s missing-persons register as the result of reports from relatives or fellow service members. As of Aug. 8, 2026, 249 people covered by the study remained on the register, another 17 had previously been listed as missing but were later removed, seven were taken off the list after being released in prisoner exchanges, and one was officially declared dead.
Nearly 90% of the known disappearances (239 out of 266) occurred in Ukrainian territories that are under Russian military occupation. The most common last known locations were Melitopol, Nova Kakhovka, Kherson, Donetsk, Berdiansk, Enerhodar, Tokmak, Oleshky, and Skadovsk. Overall, 454 of the 555 people in the study — 81.8% — were first detained in Ukraine. Another 100 were detained within Russia’s internationally recognized borders, and one was taken into custody in Kazakhstan.
As of the time the study was completed, Russian courts had sentenced 402 Ukrainians on treason, espionage, and related charges . Courts in occupied Ukrainian territories handed down 241 of those sentences — 60.1%. Among individual courts, the Southern District Military Court in Rostov-on-Don issued the largest number of convictions, with 65.
Sentences are known in only 382 of the cases. Of those, seven received life terms, while the rest were sentenced to prison terms ranging from five years to 27 years and nine months. The median sentence was 14 years. In cases where treason or espionage charges were combined with terrorism or sabotage charges, the median sentence rose to 18 years.
In 323 cases, researchers from Pervy Otdel and Parubets Analytics were able to determine certain specifics of the accusations. Just over half of those cases — 176, or 54.5% — involved allegations of collecting and passing information to Ukraine about Russian troops, military equipment, and infrastructure. Another 37 people were accused of preparing or carrying out terrorist attacks, making assassination attempts, or successfully carrying out a killing. Additionally, 34 were accused of providing financial assistance to Ukraine, 15 of sabotage targeting transportation or infrastructure, and another 15 of serving in or attempting to join the Ukrainian armed forces or other Ukrainian formations.
As of the time of the study, 534 of the 555 people remained in custody, though researchers were able to determine the exact place of detention for only 360 of them. Of those whose locations were known, 236 were being held in facilities inside Russia and another 124 in pretrial detention centers and penal colonies in occupied Ukrainian territories. Researchers said Ukrainians have also been transferred to prisons in Siberia, the Russian Far East, and the Far North.
The report’s authors stressed that 555 is not a complete count. They estimated that the names of about 30% of defendants in such cases remain unknown due to the fact that proceedings are closed and court records often omit identifying information. The study’s data are current as of Aug. 8, 2026.

articles.title: Russia demands a "strong peace" from Ukraine, but on its own terms — Peskov
articles.body:
Russia demands a "strong peace" from Ukraine, but on its own terms — Peskov
Kyiv • UNN
Putin's spokesman said that the Kremlin opposes a ceasefire and demands territorial concessions from Ukraine, its renunciation of NATO, and demilitarization.
Russia advocates for a "solid peace, peace forever, rather than a ceasefire that, essentially, will achieve nothing." Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said this in a comment to Russian "media," reports UNN.
Details
According to the Russian dictator's spokesman, "the situation in Ukraine is deteriorating every day, and this will continue."
As for Zelenskyy's statements today, obviously, the situation in Ukraine, as we have said, is deteriorating every day — both the economic situation and the situation on the fronts, and this will continue
What the Kremlin wants
Russia demands that Ukraine fully withdraw its troops from the Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia regions, as well as officially renounce any plans to integrate into NATO.
In addition, the Kremlin demands that Kyiv carry out "demilitarization," meaning complete disarmament, and "denazification" (a ban on the fabricated "Nazis" — ed.), as well as "ensuring all rights for the Russian-speaking population."
Recall
Earlier, Russian President's spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that the adoption in the United States of a law on "hellish sanctions" was an unfriendly step.

articles.title: How to cover Ukraine’s budget deficit: Zelenskyy discussed possible solutions with Denmark’s prime minister
articles.body:
How to cover Ukraine’s budget deficit: Zelenskyy discussed possible solutions with Denmark’s prime minister
Kyiv • UNN
Zelenskyy and Frederiksen discussed financial support for Ukraine, EU sanctions, and joint defense production. Denmark previously allocated $275 million for air defense.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy discussed financial support for Ukraine with Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen. In addition, they exchanged views on the European Union's sanctions policy and the expansion of defense cooperation. The head of state reported this on his official Telegram channel, UNN reports.
Details
At the very beginning, Zelenskyy emphasized that Russia's aspiration to escalate the war must be met with increased sanctions pressure.
When Russia constantly demonstrates its desire to escalate the war, the response should be stronger sanctions, not the opposite. Every name was included on the sanctions list for a reason: each of them is a reason why this war began and continues to this day, why our people are killed every day
He thanked Denmark for supporting this position and expressed hope that European partners would maintain unity and work toward the establishment of peace.
The financial resilience of Ukraine was a separate topic of the conversation. Zelenskyy and Frederiksen discussed decisions that could help cover the Ukrainian budget deficit.
The president also spoke about the situation regarding Russian attacks and Ukraine's developments to counter jet-powered "Shaheds." In addition, the parties discussed joint defense production, including the construction of new enterprises.
There is potential to expand cooperation, and we agreed to realize it
To remind you
Earlier, it became known that Denmark would allocate $275 million to Ukraine. This concerns the 31st military aid package worth $275 million. The funds will be directed toward strengthening air defense in the autumn and winter.

articles.title: Iraq extends armed groups disarmament deadline to June 2027
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Iraq extends armed groups disarmament deadline to June 2027
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi has agreed with leaders of the country's powerful pro-Iran political bloc to give armed groups until June 2027 to complete their disarmament, sources in Baghdad told The New Arab, extending a process initially expected to conclude by the end of September.
The agreement was reached with leaders of Iraq's pro-Iran Coordination Framework, which holds the largest bloc in parliament, before Al-Zaidi travelled to the United States for the UN General Assembly and talks with US officials, the sources said.
The move effectively gives powerful armed factions another nine months to bring their weapons under state control, amid continued resistance from some groups and disagreements over how the process should be implemented.
Al-Zaidi had previously committed to bringing weapons outside state control under government authority by 30 September, following attacks by pro-Iran armed groups on US bases during the war on Iran and subsequent US air strikes on their positions.
Under the new plan, the process would instead be completed by 30 June 2027, with the implementation phase expected to begin in January.
By extending the timeframe, Al-Zaidi hopes to remove the remaining justifications cited by armed factions that have refused to surrender their weapons or fully integrate into Iraq's state security forces.
A new directorate will reportedly be established within the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) to oversee the process, operating under the supervision of the Iraqi government.
The body would be responsible for receiving and cataloguing weapons, ammunition and military equipment held by armed groups, identifying where they are stored and establishing procedures governing their use.
However, the weapons would remain within facilities overseen by the PMF rather than being handed directly to the Iraqi government, a provision that could become a key point of contention with Washington.
Members and leaders of armed factions would also receive immunity from prosecution and retain the right to participate in Iraq's political process if they sign pledges to refrain from armed activity outside state authority.
Disagreement over who controls the weapons
A key dispute remains over who will ultimately control the groups' arsenals.
Washington has pushed for the Iraqi state to establish a monopoly over weapons, while the proposed arrangement would leave the PMF playing a central role in overseeing arms surrendered by the factions.
The US reportedly considers transferring weapons from faction-controlled warehouses to storage facilities that remain under PMF authority insufficient to meet its demands for weapons to be brought fully under state control.
Baghdad, however, faces considerable obstacles in forcing the issue.
Several powerful armed groups continue to resist full disarmament, while the Iraqi government has sought to avoid a military confrontation with factions that retain significant military and political influence.
Pro-Iran groups have also set a series of conditions for giving up their weapons, including the full withdrawal of US forces from Iraq and Turkish troops from northern Iraq, the restoration of what they describe as Iraq's full sovereignty over its territory, stronger Iraqi air defences and federal control over the borders of the autonomous Kurdistan region.
The dispute has complicated Al-Zaidi's attempt to fulfil his pledge to bring all weapons under state authority while avoiding a confrontation with groups that form part of the country's broader political and security establishment.
'Very difficult, indeed impossible'
Uday al-Khadran, a member of the Coordination Framework, told The New Arab that resolving the issue by the end of September had become "very difficult, indeed impossible", citing resistance among armed groups and the absence of mechanisms capable of implementing the process.
He nevertheless said the factions would eventually comply with the government's demands.
"Everyone will ultimately hand over the weapons," al-Khadran said. "But the matter requires arrangements, understandings and sufficient time to complete the process."
He added that negotiations were continuing and that the parties had yet to reach a final agreement on all aspects of the plan.
The priority, al-Khadran said, was to reach an arrangement acceptable to the parties involved that would ultimately bring weapons under state control.

articles.title: Russia attacks Ukraine with missiles and 212 drones: hits recorded at 22 locations
articles.body:
Russia attacks Ukraine with missiles and 212 drones: hits recorded at 22 locations
Russian forces attacked Ukraine with missiles of various types and 212 drones on the night of 21-22 September, while air defence forces downed 186 aerial assets.
Source: Ukraine's Air Force
Details: The Russians launched Oniks anti-ship missiles from Rostov Oblast, while Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles were fired from Kursk, Rostov and Voronezh oblasts.
Four Kalibr cruise missiles were launched from the waters of the Caspian Sea and eight Banderol/Dan-T drone missiles from the airspace over Belgorod Oblast.
The Russians also attacked with 212 Shahed drones (some jet-powered) and Parody decoy UAVs. They were launched from the Russian cities of Oryol, Millerovo, Shatalovo, Kursk and Primorsko-Akhtarsk as well as from the occupied cities of Donetsk and Hvardiiske and Chauda in Crimea.
Dnipropetrovsk, Kirovohrad and Poltava oblasts have been the main targets of the attack.
Aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare assets, unmanned systems units and mobile fire groups from Ukraine's defence forces have been involved in repelling the attack.
Quote: "As of 08:00, [Ukrainian] air defence forces had destroyed or jammed 186 aerial assets:
- 1 Kalibr cruise missile
- 8 Banderol/Dan-T drone missiles
- 177 Shahed, Gerbera and other types of drones.
Hits by missiles and attack UAVs have been recorded at 22 locations and the fall of downed aerial assets (debris) at four locations."
Background:
- Two people were killed and six injured in a Russian ballistic missile attack on the city of Dnipro on the night of 21-22 September.
- The Russians launched a large-scale attack on Poltava Oblast, hitting an industrial facility and a critical infrastructure site in the Kremenchuk district.

articles.title: Lithuania plans key substation near Russia, fortified against explosive drones
articles.body:
Lithuania plans key substation near Russia, fortified against explosive drones
VILNIUS/WARSAW, Sept 22 - Lithuania is planning defences against military drones at a key future power grid substation linking the Baltic states with western Europe in an area that intelligence sources say Russia could target with a false flag attack.
The construction plans include fencing strong enough to resist an explosives-laden truck, sensors searching for possible tunnels dug by hostile actors, and concrete "sarcophagi" for transformers to withstand any drone attack, Litgrid CEO Andrius Semeskevicius told Reuters.
"Previously, when designing our grid, we planned for natural disasters. Now, we think about all possible hybrid and non-hybrid threats", he said in an interview.
The Gizai substation, to be built some 30 km (19 miles) west of the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, will be the first new installation in the region since Russia launched its full-blown invasion of Ukraine in 2022. It will be part of a key grid section being built to ensure steady power supply to the Baltic states in case of a wider conflict.
Its route through a section of Poland and Lithuania squeezed between Russia and its ally Belarus -- the so-called Suwalki Gap -- has long caused security concerns within the NATO military alliance, of which Warsaw and Vilnius are both members.
Such concerns increased this month after a series of sabotage attacks against Germany's electricity grid that Berlin blamed on Moscow. Russia denied any involvement.
Intelligence sources told Reuters last month the region is worried about a false flag drone attack by Russia to test NATO unity. A false flag attack is an operation designed to deceive people about who is actually responsible for carrying it out.
NO ORDINARY CONCRETE
The Gizai substation will be the crucial node of the interconnection with Poland called Harmony Link, which completes the connection of the Baltic grids with the rest of the European Union after they decoupled from Russia's grid last year.
"For Lithuania, this line is absolutely crucial, it's their lifeline if the system collapses," an official from a grid company in the region told Reuters, speaking on condition of anonymity. "The timing of this decision is linked to increasing tensions in the region and rising threats of sabotage."
The substation will be spread across a 35-hectare site, so a single hit from a military drone would only harm a limited amount of equipment, Semeskevicius said.
The distance of buildings from the fence means protection "in case someone throws a Molotov cocktail inside", he added.
"We are designing Gizai for a new reality... we are protecting ourselves from multiple Shahed drones, which could crash-land with 100 kilograms of explosives", he said.
Russia uses low-cost, long-range Shahed attack drones, designed by Iran, to wreak havoc on Ukrainian military infrastructure, cities and energy facilities, depriving millions of people of heating and lighting.
"We cannot use simple concrete, it needs to be custom-made, for stronger resistance", said Semeskevicius. The right concrete has threads of plastic to reinforce it and prevent it from crumbling, he said.
The substation includes several duplicate units of key equipment, for example, so it can keep operating if one is damaged or destroyed. Replacing the bespoke equipment could take years.
"You cannot down a Shahed drone, or a drone with optical cable attached. So we need reinforced-concrete sarcophagi around equipment", said Semeskevicius.
The equipment needs to be artificially cooled down inside the sarcophagi, which adds to the cost.
"Without all this, we might not have power at all", he said.
Lithuania's military is advising Litgrid on physically securing critical energy infrastructure and resistance to modern threats, officials told Reuters.
THE MOST COSTLY INTERCONNECTION
Later this month, Lithuania will ask the EU to cover at least half of the Gizai costs, Energy Minister Lukas Savickas told Reuters.
Litgrid says the secured substation will cost at least €48 million more than planned earlier. The price could increase further if "geopolitical circumstances" worsen.
"Our consistent position is... these costs should not fall solely on our shoulders," Savickas said.
A senior Polish official echoed that view, saying countries that border Russia risk losing competitiveness if their companies are stuck with the bill for additional security.
Harmony Link cannot become "the most costly interconnection in Europe", Wojciech Wrochna, Poland's deputy energy minister in charge of strategic energy infrastructure, said, calling for the EU to boost financing of the grid security measures.
"Our European partners need to change their mindset," Wrochna told Reuters. "The issue extends beyond Harmony Link. It affects the entire energy system."
Last year the Baltic states and Poland asked the EU for €382 million to help secure key parts of the existing grid but only €112 million was granted.
The European Commission did not reply to Reuters' request for comment. REUTERS

articles.title: EU removes oligarchs from Russia sanctions list as deadline looms
articles.body:
The EU has agreed to remove two Russian billionaires, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, from its sanctions list, while extending restrictions on nearly 3,000 individuals and companies accused of supporting the war on Ukraine for the next three years.
With an end-of-Tuesday deadline looming to preserve the Russia blacklist, the EU’s 27 member states found a compromise that meant delisting the two oligarchs in spite of very few countries wanting this outcome. EU sanctions have to be approved unanimously.
France stunned and infuriated EU governments this month when it called for Usmanov, a Russian-Uzbek national, to be removed from the list on “national security” grounds, reported to refer to a prisoner exchange deal involving French nationals and Azerbaijan.
Luxembourg then asked for the same treatment for Fridman, the Russian-Israeli magnate, who is suing the Grand Duchy for $16bn (£12bn) for freezing his assets.
The exemptions angered many EU countries which believe it sets a bad precedent by allowing member states to weaken sanctions in defence of national interests.
Ukraine criticised the removal of the men from the sanctions list as unacceptable. Shortly after the decision emerged, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on social media: “No name on the sanctions list is there by accident: each one represents a reason why this war started and continues to this day.”
The Ukrainian foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, called the decision “shameful and unjustifiable” on X. “Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans,” he added.
In order to enable the delistings that many EU member states found unpalatable, it was proposed that the sanctions be rolled over for 36 months, rather than the usual six.
A spokesperson for Ireland’s EU presidency, which brokered the talks, said the bloc had reached “a difficult compromise”. They said: “Until now, these listings have been reviewed and assessed on a six-monthly basis; today’s decision to renew on a 36-month basis enhances the durability and predictability of the EU sanctions framework.”
A decision had been expected earlier this week, but Latvia’s government, facing parliamentary elections on 3 October, announced a last-minute objection to the delistings on Monday. Latvia’s prime minister, Andris Kulbergs, said late on Monday night that he could not accept the proposed compromise and instructed his foreign minister to enter talks with Paris and Brussels to find a solution.
Diplomats said Latvia had finally agreed to abstain on the two delistings. The blacklist includes Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, and foreign minister, Sergey Lavrov, as well as Duma deputies, the country’s major banks, energy companies and military industrial complex.
Senior EU officials have promised to present about 1,600 new designations – individuals and entities involved in the Russian military industrial complex – to foreign ministers next month. But the latest standoff, which followed the tortuous agreement on the EU’s 21st round of sanctions in July, suggests the process could be difficult.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Russian Drone Base in Oryol, Hits Five Launchers and Storage Facilities
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Strikes Russian Drone Base in Oryol, Hits Five Launchers and Storage Facilities
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian storage and launch site for attack drones in Russia’s Oryol region, damaging five launchers and several storage facilities, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on September 22.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the General Staff, the strike was carried out on September 21 against a facility near the settlement of Tsymbulova, which was used by Russian forces to store, prepare, and launch attack drones.
At least three drone storage facilities were hit, resulting in fires at the site. The strike also damaged a launch area used for jet-powered UAVs, as well as five drone launchers.
The General Staff said Ukrainian forces systematically target facilities used to store, prepare, and launch Russian attack drones as part of efforts to reduce Moscow’s ability to conduct strikes against civilian targets in Ukraine.
The operation follows a series of Ukrainian strikes against other Russian military assets. On September 20 and overnight into September 21, Ukrainian forces targeted a Kasta radar system valued at at least $60 million, as well as a drone command post and an area where Russian troops were concentrated.
Ukraine’s General Staff reported that the radar was struck near Pikuzy in the temporarily occupied Donetsk region. The system was identified as a Kasta-2E2 (39N6), a mobile radar designed to detect low-flying aircraft, missiles, and unmanned aerial vehicles at ranges of up to 150 kilometers.
Ukrainian strikes have also targeted Russia’s oil infrastructure. A fire broke out at the Kuibyshev Oil Refinery in Russia’s Samara region following an overnight Ukrainian drone attack on September 22, with preliminary analysis suggesting that one of the facility’s processing units was damaged, Russian media outlet ASTRA reported.
Residents of the Samara region reported hearing explosions overnight. After analyzing eyewitness footage, ASTRA identified the Kuibyshev refinery as the apparent target, with footage showing a fire at the facility.

articles.title: Trump announced a “massive” potash deal with Belarus—Lukashenka said the same day there is no spare potash to sell
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump announced a "massive deal" to buy Belarusian potash at prices far below what the US pays Canada, but Belarusian dictator Alyaksandr Lukashenka publicly contradicted him the same day, saying Belarus has no spare volumes to sell.
Washington has spent a year courting Lukashenka with sanctions relief and envoy visits in pursuit of both prisoner releases and trade openings—but the potash episode shows the limits of that courtship when the dictator's own supply chain cannot deliver what the US President has already promised his voters.
Trump promised cheaper potash for American farmers
Trump wrote on Truth Social on 21 September:
"The United States is working on a massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash from Belarus. The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers."
Potash is a key ingredient in fertilizer. Canada is the world's largest supplier—the US takes 53% of Canadian potash exports, and 80% of the potash American farms use comes from Canada. Canadian potash remains exempt from US tariffs despite the ongoing trade war between the two countries.
The announcement came as Trump's trade dispute with Ottawa deepened—he recently called Canada a "terrible trade partner," and on 16 September European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen offered Canada associate EU membership, which Trump said could be a "hostile act."
Lukashenka said all output is contracted
The same day, Lukashenka told officials Belarus cannot deliver. "Even if we wanted to supply potash to other, Western markets, we simply do not have those volumes—everything is contracted," he said during a meeting with the head of Belarus's State Customs Committee, Uladzimir Arlouski.
Arlouski reported that 85% of all Belarusian exports and imports now move eastward—primarily to China, other Asian countries, and Russia. Budget revenues grew almost 3.5% over eight months, and 5.2% so far this month.
A deal built on sanctions relief and prisoner swaps
The potash announcement followed a year-long US effort to engage Lukashenka. Washington lifted sanctions on Belarus's potash industry in exchange for the release of hundreds of political prisoners. US special envoy John Cole has played the central role, meeting Lukashenka last week and securing the release of 25 prisoners—far fewer than the 200 he had previously promised.
Over the course of Cole's effort, at least several hundred people have been freed, among them Nobel Peace Prize laureate Ales Bialiatski and Siarhei Tsikhanouski, husband of the internationally recognized winner of Belarus's 2020 presidential election. But human rights groups and freed prisoners say Lukashenka runs a "carousel"—arresting new political opponents to replace the ones he releases. Lukashenka denied this. "There are no political prisoners in Belarus," he claimed during last week's meeting with Cole.
With US midterms six weeks away on 3 November and the Republican Party struggling in the polls, Trump has been scrambling for wins on fuel and food prices. The same week, he urged Zelenskyy to stop hitting Russian refineries, blaming Ukraine rather than his own war with Iran for record US diesel prices—a move a senior European official told Politico was a search for "scapegoats."

articles.title: Trump will pressure Zelenskyy in New York, demanding concessions regarding strikes on Russia – The Guardian
articles.body:
Trump will pressure Zelenskyy in New York, demanding concessions regarding strikes on Russia – The Guardian
Kyiv • UNN
Trump plans to pressure Zelenskyy over a mutual cessation of strikes on energy infrastructure. Kyiv is ready to take steps if Russia stops the attacks.
U.S. President Donald Trump is expected to insist on an agreement on a mutual halt to Ukrainian and Russian strikes against energy infrastructure during his meeting with Volodymyr Zelenskyy in New York. The Guardian reports, according to UNN.
Details
The presidents’ meeting is scheduled to take place on Tuesday on the sidelines of the high-level week of the United Nations General Assembly. The publication links Trump’s position, in particular, to the sharp rise in global diesel prices.
Ukraine has recently stepped up long-range strikes against Russia’s energy infrastructure. Last weekend, Ukrainian forces carried out a large-scale attack on the Moscow region, during which a major oil refinery in Moscow was hit.
Trump calls for strikes on Russian oil refineries to stop
On Monday, Trump said that Ukraine’s strikes had knocked out a significant portion of Russia’s diesel production capacity. At the same time, the U.S. president called on Kyiv to stop such attacks because of a fuel shortage on the global market.
According to The Guardian, during his visit to Ireland last week, Trump also urged Zelenskyy not to attack Russian diesel production facilities. On Sunday, the presidents held a phone call during which, according to the Financial Times, the issue of diesel fuel was one of the main topics.
The average price of diesel fuel in the United States reached a record $6.50 per gallon on Monday, compared with $3.19 a year earlier. Prices rose amid the war with Iran, shipping restrictions through the Strait of Hormuz, and a reduction in Russian refining capacity.
Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was ready for reciprocal de-escalation measures if Russia stopped strikes against Ukrainian energy facilities, critical infrastructure, and facilities connected with food exports.
Last week, Trump said that an agreement on an energy truce between Ukraine and Russia had allegedly been reached. However, as The Guardian notes, the agreement was not actually finalized, and Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy and other critical infrastructure continued.

articles.title: Trump and Iran Exchange Threats as Leaders Converge for Key U.N. Gathering. Can the Meeting Cool Rising Tensions?
articles.body:
Delegations from the U.S. and Iran are traveling to New York for the world’s largest diplomatic gathering this week in what experts say could be a key moment for determining the direction of the Iran war nearly seven months in.
Tensions between the warring countries are mounting ahead of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), with Iranian leaders and President Donald Trump exchanging a fresh round of threats.
Trump on Sunday weighed whether he should “blow the entire nation up” in an interview with Fox News, warning that Iran “better behave” and saying that “very big things” would happen in the war, without offering more detail. According to the outlet, Trump described his options as “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically, or making a deal.”
A spokesperson for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Hossein Mohebbi, responded with a warning that if the U.S. were to launch fresh attacks against Iran, Tehran would use “new weapons and capabilities,” according to Iran's Fars news agency. “If a new aggression takes place, we will definitely change the weapons and geography of the war,” Mohebbi said.
The threats come after active hostilities in the conflict resumed in the last month when the U.S. and Iran traded fresh strikes amid tensions over the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway in the global oil market. Meaningful negotiations between the two countries have meanwhile been stalled for weeks following the breakdown of a memorandum of understanding leaders signed in June. And Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels have further shaken the Gulf region by launching attacks against Saudi Arabia and capturing Perim Island, a strategic foothold in the Bab El-Mandeb Strait, another vital maritime trade route in the region.
Experts tell TIME that the U.N. General Assembly gathering, where delegations from Iran, the U.S., and key Gulf states will be in attendance, could offer a critical chance to deescalate the situation and attempt to revive peace efforts—although making progress in negotiations could be an uphill battle.
“This week in New York, there is an opportunity, especially for the mediating countries, to try to prevent tensions from once again spiraling, and potentially this time spiraling out of control,” says Ali Vaez, the deputy program director for the Middle East and North Africa at the International Crisis Group. “It's the last best opportunity to try to prevent an escalation either in October or in November.”
What to expect at this week’s U.N. General Assembly
Top officials from the U.S. and Iran will be present at the U.N. meeting this week, including Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and U.S. ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi will be in attendance as part of a slimmed-down delegation from the country. Both Trump and Pezeshkian are set to deliver addresses to the assembly.
Vaez says, however, that any effort to revive peace talks between the two countries during the event will largely rely on mediation by Gulf states.
Trump is set to hold talks with leaders from the Gulf Cooperation Council—a regional alliance including Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman, and Bahrain—on the sidelines of the gathering in the coming days. Sources with knowledge of the anticipated meeting told Axios, which first reported the news, that discussions are expected to concern next steps in the war with Iran, with a focus on U.S. ideas for a strategy after the conflict concludes.
Vaez believes that the Qataris could play a leading role in mediation efforts, with the support of countries such as Saudi Arabia, Oman, Turkey, Pakistan, and Egypt.
“It all depends on whether the mediating countries would be able to find a mutually acceptable formula,” he says of the possibility of the U.S. and Iran coming to some kind of agreement. “Because at this moment, both sides are in a zero-sum situation in which there is literally no overlap between what the Iranians demand and what the U.S. is seeking to achieve.”
Given what he characterized as maximalist demands from both the U.S. and Iran, Vaez contends that “some sort of a sweetener,” or incentive, must be given to each side for a deal to be reached, which he says may come in the form of revisions to the now-expired memorandum of understanding.
Sanam Valki, director of the Middle East and North Africa Programme at the policy institute Chatham House, agrees that it is far more likely that Gulf states mediate between Iran and the U.S. But, she adds, a direct exchange between U.S. and Iranian delegations is also a possibility—albeit a very slim one.
“The big question out there is: Will there be some sort of surprise encounter between the Iranians and the U.S.?” Valki says.
Trump told Fox News’ Trey Yingst on Sunday that he would be willing to meet with Pezeshkian during the U.N. gathering.
Beyond either mediated or direct discussions during the event, another potential outcome of this week’s General Assembly meeting is a United Nations Security Council Resolution regarding the Iran conflict, Vaez says. Unlike a memorandum of understanding like the one the U.S. and Iran previously reached, a security resolution would be legally binding by international law and would compel both parties to abide by certain conditions in the war.
Adopting a resolution would require the votes of at least nine out of the 15 members of the security council. And as a complicating factor, the U.S.—as well as the other four permanent members—would have the ability to defeat any such measure by casting a veto.
How could the U.N. meeting impact the Iran war moving forward?
“This is a very important week at UNGA for regional states, as well as the Iranians themselves, to try and roll back or manage how things evolve,” Valki tells TIME. “The President is very clearly weighing and considering the military options that are on his desk, which include not just responding to the Houthis, but another round of serious and severe strikes against the Islamic Republic.”
If a direct exchange between the U.S. and Iranian delegations does unexpectedly occur during the gathering, she says, “it's a big deal. It's a big outcome. It means that the Iranian president is willing to risk his standing at home, attacks at home, in order to stave off a serious military attack and build a direct lifeline to the Trump team.”
Up until now, both sides have sought “maximalist outcomes with minimal concessions,” Valki says. But Iran, through direct conversation with the U.S. delegation, could “signal a more transformational type of policy outreach, rather than the defensive reaction of traditional hardliners in the country.”
On Trump’s end, Vaez says the President could potentially make concessions to Iran by removing naval blockades on Iranian ports, rolling back sanctions against Tehran, or returning access to certain frozen assets. “That's what the President can put on the table … The most important thing for Iranians is economic reprieve and that's precisely where President Trump has tremendous leverage.”
A security council resolution, meanwhile, “could provide a degree of assurance about the sustainability of a new understanding between Iran and the U.S.,” Vaez says. He adds that through such a resolution, the U.N. could also establish an “observer mission”—what he describes as “an established mechanism that could look into disputes and adjudicate” if there are disagreements over alleged violations of the resolution, as there were previously over June’s memorandum of understanding.
Vaez stresses, though, that the odds of this week’s gathering resulting in a meaningful breakthrough in the stalled negotiations appears unlikely.
“There are very serious differences, and there's deep mistrust,” he says. “And so that's why I'm not very optimistic.”

articles.title: Rostec supplies latest Zubr anti-drone systems to military
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 22. /TASS/. Rostec’s High Precision Systems Holding Company has delivered the latest Zubr anti-drone systems to the Russian Defense Ministry, which are designed to counter small, low-flying targets, the state corporation reported.
"The High Precision Holding of the Rostec State Corporation, has supplied the Russian Defense Ministry with the latest Zubr air defense systems intended to protect important facilities from small, low-flying threats. They are capable of independently detecting and tracking unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and can also be integrated into a unified, layered anti-drone defense system," the state corporation stated.
Rostec said that the Zubr is a close-in air defense system operating in the lower airspace where a rapid response to the appearance of UAVs and loitering munitions is crucial.
"The Zubr can be used both independently or integrated into a unified anti-drone defense architecture to build a layered air defense system for facilities. The system also serves as the last line of defense for large facilities, forming a unified air defense perimeter with them, including alongside the Pantsir missile systems," the state corporation specified.
In addition, the system is easy to maintain in the field and can be deployed rapidly. This is particularly important for a system that must remain constantly combat-ready, including at remote and poorly equipped positions, Rostec noted.
"The system developed by High Precision Systems is equipped with everything necessary for round-the-clock detection of drones of any size and their automatic tracking. Once the Zubr locks onto an aerial target, it engulfs it in a dense barrage of fire. As a result, at the final line of defense, where the system comes into play, enemy drones have virtually no chance of survival. "Zubr’s effectiveness is confirmed by its combat deployment experience and the steadily growing number of real targets destroyed by the system," said Bekkhan Ozdoyev, industrial director of Rostec’s Armament Cluster and board member of the Union of Russian Machine-Building Enterprises.

articles.title: Ukraine shoots down Russian drones by hundred thousand: 350,000 this year, filmed and verified hit by hit in DELTA
articles.body:
Ukraine's forces have shot down more than 350,000 Russian drones since the start of the year. The count, some 220,000 fixed-wing drones, 100,000 quadcopters, and 31,000 long-range Gerans, was filmed hit by hit in the DELTA combat system and verified by the Brave1 defense-innovation cluster, the Defense Ministry said.
Meanwhile, Russia is now threatening NATO countries directly, its drones probing Polish and Baltic skies, and those countries manage to down only a small fraction of what crosses their borders. In one incursion, Poland shot down just four of about 19 Russian drones.
Ukraine's 350,000 is the record of a force that has had to master drone defense at an industrial scale, night after night.
The tally runs to hundreds of thousands
Most of the kills belong to the Defense Forces' unmanned-systems units, which downed more than 320,000 Russian fixed-wing and copter drones. Those units, together with mobile fire groups and army aviation, also brought down faster Geran-type attack drones.
The pace has been relentless: in August alone, Ukraine destroyed some 35,000 fixed-wing drones and nearly 24,000 copters, the ministry said.
DELTA verifies every hit
Every downing is logged and confirmed in DELTA, the digital system Ukraine uses to run the battlefield, and which the ministry calls a key to its edge over Russia. Filming and verifying each kill lets commanders study how it was done and scale up whatever works.
The purpose is concrete: knocking down fixed-wing drones blinds Russian reconnaissance, and blunts strikes on cities and critical infrastructure, while downing copters keeps Russia from finding and hitting front-line positions. Each drone stopped, the ministry says, is potentially the life of a Ukrainian soldier or civilian saved.
The same threat now shadows NATO
That threat is spreading. Prime Minister Donald Tusk told Poland's parliament that intelligence points to Russian plans for drone and missile strikes on countries backing Ukraine.
The allies being warned are the ones that have struggled to stop even a handful of drones, while Ukraine, out of necessity, has learned to bring them down by the hundred thousand.
